conflicts.issue: Passage of Modified SCAD UDO Text Amendment via Late-Night Dais Exclusion Motion
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 at 11:45 PM over whether to pass a selectively amended version of SCAD drafted orally on the dais from Attachment M or vote the private developer application down and allow staff to return with clean ordinance text.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve staff-recommended SCAD provisions tonight while carving out Topic 6, PATH, and disputed clauses for the UDO rewrite.
side_a_arguments: Passing uncontroversial staff-recommended reforms like detached row houses now avoids waiting years for the UDO rewrite.
Carving out specific UDO paragraph numbers recommended against by staff—plus Topic 6 and PATH—addresses major task force objections.
Council retains authority to monitor impacts and amend provisions later, as it did with Expanding Housing Choices.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the private application as drafted or defer until staff returns with clear, finalized ordinance language for public review.
side_b_arguments: Reading out dozens of UDO section exclusions orally near midnight is confusing ('mumbly jumbly') and a disservice to residents and staff.
Voting SCAD down does not prevent staff from bringing back consensus items in clean ordinance form.
Major affordable housing advocates opposed PATH and task force discussions were incomplete.
conflicts.resolution: Both the selective SCAD ordinance motion and its consistency statement passed 4-3 by hand vote.

conflicts.issue: Perry Farm Consolidated Annexation and PDR 3.155 Rezoning (Item 24)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 over annexing and rezoning the Perry Farm property in the Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation, utility extension, and PDR 3.155 rezoning with watershed protections.
side_a_arguments: The property already carries county Residential Rural zoning and is developable regardless of annexation.
Environmental proffers go beyond UDO minimums while maintaining the 24%/70% impervious limits and 100-foot/50-foot stream buffers.
Residents seeking pure natural heritage preservation would need to pursue nonprofit land acquisition.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose annexation and rezoning due to environmental, water, blasting, and infrastructure concerns.
side_b_arguments: Nearby county residential wells are impaired and county/city water availability remains unresolved.
Blasting impacts, natural heritage loss, and unfunded taxpayer transportation burdens need deeper scrutiny.
State law still classifies the annexation as non-contiguous based on its status at initial filing.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation/utility extension and PDR 3.155 rezoning passed 4-3; consistency statement passed 6-1.

conflicts.issue: Fletcher Crossing (Item 17) Southeast Durham Townhouse Density vs. Road and Stormwater Infrastructure
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 on annexing and rezoning 9.47 acres at 707 S. Mineral Springs Road for 80 townhouses, debating housing supply and diverse housing types against narrow road infrastructure, transit absence, and Planning Commission's 5-4 denial.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve Fletcher Crossing to add 80 missing-middle townhomes at 8.347 units per acre rather than 16 expensive single-family homes.
side_a_arguments: The draft Place Type map designates the area as Mixed Residential Neighborhood, which townhomes help diversify.
16 large-lot single-family homes by right would cost around $800,000 compared to mid-$300k/low-$400k townhomes.
The developer is dedicating 10 feet of right-of-way along Mineral Springs and Holder Roads and preserving rear tree cover and wetlands.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning due to inadequate road and transit infrastructure, neighborhood flooding, and lack of small-area planning or affordable housing.
side_b_arguments: Narrow 10-foot lanes, lack of streetlights or transit, and downstream Holder Road flooding show the infrastructure is not ready for cumulative density.
Without small-area planning or affordable housing proffers, piecemeal upzonings shift infrastructure burdens onto existing residents.
The Planning Commission recommended denial 5-4 and Council should respect differing neighborhood impacts across projects.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: 631 & 633 Clayton Road (Item 20) Townhouse Rezoning and Missing Legistar Development Plan Exhibit
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 on annexing and rezoning 7.7 acres across from Southern High School for 61 townhouses (with 9 at <=80% AMI) after adjacent homeowner opposition and discovery that the development plan map was missing from the public Legistar packet.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 61-townhome project with nine income-restricted units as an appropriate infill transition near Southern High School.
side_a_arguments: Planning Commission recommended approval 6-2 and the project proffers nine affordable units at 80% AMI plus enhanced erosion-control flocculents.
A 30-foot, 60%-opacity buffer separates townhomes from the neighboring Wiggins residence, and line-of-sight concerns alone do not justify denial.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose voting on the rezoning while the development plan building-envelope exhibit was omitted from the public Legistar file and adjacent long-time residents oppose.
side_b_arguments: Staff acknowledged an oversight left the development plan attachment out of Legistar, depriving residents and Council of exact building-envelope and sightline details.
Adjacent property owner Tanisha Wiggins testified the townhomes clash with long-established single-family homes on Clayton Road.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Immediate ~$8M / 2-Cent Tax Increase for Missed FY 2021 Employee Step Raises vs. Waiting for Pay Study in FY 2023-24 Budget
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 on both Mayor Elaine O'Neal's priority raise motion and final adoption of the $600M FY 2023-24 budget over whether to immediately raise property taxes by 2 cents (~$8M) to restore a missed COVID-era step raise or complete a comprehensive pay study first.
conflicts.side_a_position: Immediately fund the missed FY 2021 step raise (~$8M / 2-cent tax hike) for firefighters, police, and all city employees in the FY 2023-24 budget.
side_a_arguments: Firefighters and city workers already waited through COVID freezes and 2016 study placement gaps, hurting retention and morale.
Withholding the step increase while prioritizing other spending places budget balancing on the backs of city staff.
A 2-cent tax increase is manageable and can be offset for low-income homeowners via the property tax grant program.
conflicts.side_b_position: Pass the balanced $600M budget with a 6-8% pay increase and no property tax hike now, and address structural step compression after a comprehensive pay study.
side_b_arguments: Adding an unvetted $8M obligation and 2-cent tax hike on top of the County's 3-cent increase after telling residents there was no tax hike is fiscally irresponsible and regressive during a housing crisis.
The proposed budget already includes a 6-8% pay increase alongside major investments in HEART, Vision Zero, sidewalks, and Hayti.
Major compensation adjustments require a pay study covering all employees—including 911 operators and non-step staff—rather than ad hoc floor amendments.
conflicts.resolution: Immediate raise motion failed 3-4; FY 2023-24 budget passed 4-3.

conflicts.issue: Streets at Southpoint Mall #2 (Item 44) On-Site Affordable Housing and Binding Community Benefits Agreement
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-2 on rezoning the Streets at Southpoint Mall for 1,382 market-rate apartments, office, retail, and hotel expansion, debating whether to approve with a $1M housing-fund proffer or continue the case for binding on-site affordable housing and local-hiring commitments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Southpoint redevelopment with $1M to the Affordable Housing Loan Fund, $23,000 to DPS, and transit/bikeway upgrades to preserve Durham's top tax engine.
side_a_arguments: Southpoint generates $14M annually in city/county taxes with 71% of visitors coming from outside Durham, and delaying risks losing investment to Wake County.
Affordable housing partners testified that structured parking and non-QCT status make on-site LIHTC units financially unviable without scarce public subsidy.
Improved GoTriangle/GoDurham stops, park-and-ride spaces, and Triangle Bikeway easements deliver major transit benefits.
conflicts.side_b_position: Continue the hearing to negotiate a formal development agreement capturing on-site affordable units or land donation and enforceable local-hiring/MWBE commitments.
side_b_arguments: Brookfield built on-site affordable housing in DC, New York, and Jersey City, yet offered zero on-site units for Southpoint's 2,000 retail workers.
Promises on local hiring and supplier diversity cannot be enforced through zoning proffers and require a binding statutory development agreement.
conflicts.resolution: Applicant declined a further continuance; UEA and zoning motions passed 5-2 and consistency passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Rezoning of RS-20 and Commercial General Parcel to PDR 13.024 (90-Unit Multifamily Infill near 15-501 and West Cornwallis Road)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 on approving a 90-unit predominantly studio and one-bedroom apartment rezoning with five 60%-AMI units and a $100,000 housing fund proffer.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the PDR 13.024 rezoning to allow 90 infill apartments with five 60%-AMI affordable units and $100,000 for the Dedicated Housing Fund.
side_a_arguments: Infill density accommodates urban growth more sustainably than suburban sprawl or the by-right alternative of six single-family homes plus a 5,000-square-foot fast-food drive-thru.
Transportation analysis found negligible intersection delay (LOS B/C at 15-501 and West Cornwallis) and trip generation below the 150 peak-hour trip TIA threshold.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the PDR 13.024 rezoning.
side_b_arguments: Planner notes flagged applicant disregard for local community engagement and neighborhood concerns.
Dissenters questioned traffic level-of-service findings and how school and school-bus impacts were estimated for 90 new residential units.
conflicts.resolution: Rezoning passed 4-3; the accompanying NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement passed 6-1 with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman dissenting.

conflicts.issue: One More Carolinas LLC Annexation and PDR 4.680 Rezoning Amid Creek Sediment Concerns
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 on annexing and rezoning land for roughly 420 homes in the Falls/Jordan District B watershed after residents presented turbid sink water and complained of blood-red creek runoff.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and PDR 4.680 rezoning to allow ~420 homes without delaying development over unverified causation claims.
side_a_arguments: The creek has been impaired historically, and opponents have not presented scientific evidence linking this project or recent development activity to increased impairment.
Blanket 'slow down building' arguments do not resolve technical jurisdictional responsibilities, which planning and county staff are working to clarify.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the annexation and rezoning until stronger sedimentation/erosion protections and resident water-quality concerns are addressed.
side_b_arguments: Residents cannot afford private laboratory testing for turbid sink water and blood-red creek runoff and should not have their concerns dismissed as antagonistic.
Council has repeatedly asked developers to proffer compliance with Durham County's stronger sedimentation and erosion control amendments before approval.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and PDR 4.680 rezoning both passed 4-3; the statutory consistency statement subsequently passed 6-1 with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman dissenting.

conflicts.issue: Wilkinson Estates Annexation and PDR 3.850 Rezoning (Community Benefits, Infrastructure, and Growth Approvals)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 on annexing and rezoning the 185-townhome Wilkinson Estates development, pitting members who viewed widened stream buffers, an increased $24,000 DPS proffer, and tax-revenue/housing supply as sufficient against members demanding stronger community benefits and infrastructure readiness before approving suburban growth.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Wilkinson Estates annexation and PDR 3.850 rezoning with widened stream buffers and the increased $24,000 DPS proffer.
side_a_arguments: Widened stream buffers protect environmental features while keeping buildable density reasonable at roughly 5.28 units per acre.
Halting development approvals until roads and infrastructure are expanded is unrealistic and would starve the city budget of tax revenue needed for neglected neighborhoods and schools.
The applicant increased its one-time Durham Public Schools proffer from $5,000 to $24,000 prior to certificate of occupancy.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the annexation and rezoning until stronger community benefits and infrastructure protections are secured.
side_b_arguments: Current proffers and community benefits are inadequate, and sending inadequate proposals back can yield better outcomes for residents.
Continued residential approvals strain local schools and roads without commensurate infrastructure improvements.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and PDR 3.850 rezoning both passed 5-2; the NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Windell at Crescent: Compact Neighborhood Density Without On-Site Affordable Units or Transit
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 on annexing and rezoning Windell at Crescent for 219 apartments in a designated compact neighborhood without Light Rail transit or on-site income-restricted units.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 219-unit development with $200,000 affordable housing and $39,000 DPS proffers to add market-rate density outside gentrifying inner-city neighborhoods.
side_a_arguments: Adding walkable density on the periphery relieves displacement pressure on historic neighborhoods like Walltown.
State law restricts mandatory inclusionary zoning, making voluntary housing fund and school contributions practical levers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject annexing and granting compact-neighborhood density when Light Rail has disappeared and zero affordable units are provided on site.
side_b_arguments: City transit staff confirmed no transit line currently connects 15-501 and NC 54 through the area after Light Rail cancellation.
An earlier density-bonus/development-agreement framework had attempted to secure on-site affordability before being replaced by market-rate RCD.
conflicts.resolution: Both the annexation and RCD rezoning motions passed 5-2.

conflicts.issue: ShotSpotter Gunshot-Detection One-Year Pilot Approval
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-2 to launch the $197,500 one-year ShotSpotter acoustic gunshot-detection pilot after sharp disagreement over effectiveness, civil liberties, and police deployment in Black and brown neighborhoods.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the vetted one-year pilot to test whether acoustic gunfire detection speeds emergency medical response and evidence collection.
side_a_arguments: Independent evaluation by Duke's Wilson Center will measure real Durham data before any permanent renewal.
Faster alerts can locate shooting victims even when no 911 call is made.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose ShotSpotter and invest instead in proven root-cause violence prevention.
side_b_arguments: Other cities found high false-positive rates, minimal violence reduction, and heightened unnecessary police encounters in Black and brown neighborhoods.
$197,500 would yield greater safety returns in youth programs, mental health, and violence interruption.
conflicts.resolution: The ShotSpotter contract passed 5-2.

conflicts.issue: 1409 Doc Nichols Road Rural Annexation, Blasting/Well Water Impacts, and Housing Supply
conflicts.summary: Following a 5-5 Planning Commission tie, Council passed 1409 Doc Nichols Road 5-2 while splitting over neighbor reports of well turbidity, blasting, and Highway 98 traffic versus housing supply and three completed Habitat townhomes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 60-townhome development given upgraded Habitat, stormwater, and erosion proffers and urgent regional housing demand.
side_a_arguments: Denying the rezoning leaves worse outcomes—either luxury single-family homes on well/septic or warehouses—while restricting supply drives downtown rents upward.
The developer added three completed Habitat townhomes, double silt fencing, and 100-year stormwater ponds.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose annexing County parcels lacking city water/sewer protections and infrastructure capacity for surrounding rural residents.
side_b_arguments: Existing County residents face well-water sediment and blasting fears without automatic city utility extensions or pre-blast inspections.
Cumulative eastern annexations outpace roads, schools, and emergency response planning.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 5-2; consistency passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: 7926 Massey Chapel Road Townhomes Compatibility and Traffic Near Southpoint
conflicts.summary: Following a 7-7 Planning Commission tie, Council split 4-3 on approving 28 townhomes squeezed between rural homes and Southpoint retail.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve 28 transitional townhomes with one Habitat unit, sidewalk to the American Tobacco Trail, and 100-year stormwater controls rather than four million-dollar by-right houses.
side_a_arguments: Reducing density from 40 to 28 units and extending public water/sewer to neighbors with failing septic provides meaningful mitigation.
Townhomes near retail and the American Tobacco Trail are far more attainable than $1M single-family estates.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the rezoning due to neighborhood traffic congestion, flood-zone/stormwater concerns, height transition, and unverified sidewalk feasibility.
side_b_arguments: Southpoint weekend traffic already congests Massey Chapel Road, and no traffic study was required below 150 peak trips.
Neighbors disputed site elevation/light-pole spillover and questioned NCDOT approval for sidewalks.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency passed 5-2 after correcting clicker errors.

conflicts.issue: Infill Housing Density vs. Infrastructure Capacity and Geotechnical Risk at 301 & 401 Infinity Road
conflicts.summary: Council deadlocked 3-3 on rezoning 18.1 acres on Infinity Road for 99 townhomes and 5,000 sq ft of office, pitting proponents of infill density inside the proposed Urban Growth Boundary against opponents citing severe traffic delays, un-funded road upgrades, and Eno River rock/stormwater risks.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the infill townhouse and office rezoning as consistent with the draft Comprehensive Plan and necessary to grow inward inside an urban growth boundary.
side_a_arguments: Limiting outward sprawl via an Urban Growth Boundary requires accepting higher infill density within existing boundaries.
Withholding development until NCDOT funds every road project would stall municipal growth and reduce the city's priority for state SPOT 7 transportation intervention.
The applicant offered affordable housing and school fund contributions and committed to geotechnical borings prior to construction.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning due to unfunded road safety deficiencies on Infinity Road/Roxboro Street, lack of pre-zoning geotechnical testing, and neighborhood/environmental strain.
side_b_arguments: Transportation staff confirmed the Infinity/Roxboro project was dropped from the adopted STIP with no current funding.
Neighbors reported 5-to-10-minute delays exiting driveways and single-access bottlenecks, plus bedrock and runoff problems that stalled the adjacent Rocky Creek site.
No geotechnical study had been completed prior to the rezoning vote.
conflicts.resolution: Rezoning motion failed on a 3-3 tie.

conflicts.issue: Kemp Road Residential Annexation East of Draft Infrastructure Growth Boundary
conflicts.summary: Council split 2-4 over whether to approve a consolidated annexation and utility extension agreement east of Kemp Road ahead of finalized Comprehensive Plan/infrastructure rules and Fire Station 21 construction.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and utility extension agreement based on its project merits and fire-permit condition rather than uncodified draft policy lines.
side_a_arguments: The draft growth-boundary guidance is not yet codified law and Council should not cede decision-making to draft staff proposals.
Durham cannot legally enact a development moratorium and is one of the fastest-growing cities in the country.
The developer proffered not to seek building permits until Fire Station 21 permits are applied for, and Stations 8 and 17 are within 4-5 minutes via mutual aid.
Opposing growth under slogans like 'preserve rural Durham' can function as coded resistance to urbanization, and supporters should not be accused of being in developers' pockets.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject annexation east of Kemp Road until municipal infrastructure, fire coverage, and adopted growth policies are in place.
side_b_arguments: Planning staff are neutral arbiters whose guidance advises against building east of Kemp Road until infrastructure capacity improves.
Approving one project across the line creates a domino effect into unready areas, repeating past 4-3 Olive Branch Road rezoning controversies.
Concerns remained over 600-foot resident notification delivery and an earlier proposed fire station site across a stream that proved unviable.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to annex and authorize the Utility Extension Agreement failed 2-4 at 03:19:37, rendering the companion rezoning and consistency motions without jurisdiction.

conflicts.issue: 5909 & 6301 Leesville Road Mass Grading, Erosion Control ('Tomato Soup'), Well Water, and Growth vs. Housing Supply
conflicts.summary: Following a 9-1 Planning Commission recommendation of denial and over two hours of resident opposition, Council split 4-3 on annexing and rezoning 88 acres on Leesville Road for 330 townhomes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 330 townhomes with strengthened erosion, mass-grading, school, and housing proffers rather than leave the land to expensive well-and-septic estates or industrial uses.
side_a_arguments: Modern stormwater controls necessitate some mass grading, and the applicant added a 50% simultaneous mass-grading cap, 50% open space, $45,000 DPS contribution, and 10 affordable units.
With Durham's rents rising at the third-fastest rate nationally, blocking suburban housing pushes higher-income buyers into existing inner-city neighborhoods.
conflicts.side_b_position: Opponents and dissenting Council members argued mass grading, blasting, flocculants, and strained roads/schools impose severe environmental and taxpayer burdens on Leesville residents.
side_b_arguments: County residents forced onto bottled water due to well sediment and 'tomato soup' creek runoff lack automatic protection or city water access.

Mayor Elaine O'Neal stated she could not vote yes until Council completed its housing deep dive to understand cumulative environmental and infrastructure impacts; DeDreana Freeman argued city taxpayers bear annexation infrastructure costs while inspectors rely on complaint-driven enforcement.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3 by raised hand vote; consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 15, 2022 at 7 p.m. (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Griffin Residential Tract Annexation, Mass Grading Limits, Affordable Townhome Readiness, and Development Pause
conflicts.summary: Council deadlocked 3-3 over whether to annex the Griffin Residential Tract and extend utilities amid concerns over stormwater runoff from unlimited mass grading, affordable townhouse execution by Habitat for Humanity, and whether withholding approvals until future Comprehensive Plan policies are adopted constitutes an improper moratorium.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and utility extension rather than imposing an implicit moratorium
side_a_arguments: Council members are elected to make clear yes-or-no decisions on individual proposals rather than halting approvals until future policies are written.
Withholding approvals until unanswered policy questions are resolved amounts to an implicit moratorium.
Design commitments require any affordable townhomes to meet the same material and design standards as market-rate units, and members should debate without alleging opposing votes cause harm.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny annexation pending mass-grading limits, stormwater protections, and deeper housing policy review
side_b_arguments: Current UDO rules place zero limits on mass grading, creating stormwater runoff risks in the Southeast Durham and Falls/Jordan watershed area.
Questions remain about Habitat for Humanity's executive transition, funding, and ability to build affordable townhomes matching market-rate design commitments.
Pausing approval causes no harm and gives Council and the community time to establish updated housing and environmental standards.
conflicts.resolution: Motion 1 failed on a 3-3 tie vote at 02:49:44, leaving the property outside city jurisdiction and rendering the rezoning and consistency statement motions moot.

conflicts.issue: Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2 Rural Infrastructure, Blasting, and Housing Supply
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 over annexing and rezoning rural-edge land for 166 Epcon courtyard units amid neighbor testimony on well turbidity, dynamite blasting, and strained fire/EMS capacity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the revised 166-unit community because housing supply, senior-accessible floor plans, 33% tree save, and affordable proffers outweigh sprawl concerns.
side_a_arguments: The applicant substantially improved the 2021 plan with 33% tree preservation, zero stream crossings, and senior-friendly ground-floor units.
Stopping new housing on the urban edge worsens displacement and rents inside the urban core.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or pause outer-county annexations where cumulative blasting, well contamination, road congestion, and missing public infrastructure remain unresolved.
side_b_arguments: Neighbors near Doc Nichols and Olive Branch Roads reported sediment-laden well water, foundation concerns, and uninspected homes during blasting.
Rural roads and emergency services (EMS, schools, fire) lack an actionable capacity plan to absorb thousands of cumulative annexed units.
conflicts.resolution: The annexation and rezoning motions passed 4-3 by raised hand vote; the consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Item 16: Adopt Annexation Ordinance for Colvard Farms Tract (S.L. 2014-47)
conflicts.summary: Moved by Leonardo Williams and seconded by DeDreana Freeman for procedural disposition, the annexation of Colvard Farms failed after an electronic clicker glitch prompted a hand vote in which zero members voted aye and Mayor O'Neal announced five no votes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 0-5)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (0-5)

conflicts.issue: Smallwood Townhouses Compatibility Adjacent to FedEx Hub and Pedestrian Easement Paving
conflicts.summary: Council split 6-1 over approving residential townhouses immediately adjacent to an active FedEx freight facility without a sound wall or guaranteed paved path in the cemetery easement.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Planning Commission-recommended project, shared stormwater upgrades, and cemetery easement.
side_a_arguments: The applicant worked out a shared stormwater facility with All Saints UMC and proffered a 20-foot public access easement per Planning Commission feedback.
It is not the Council's role to shield buyers or developers from obvious adjacent industrial uses visible on site, and late-stage requests like a sound wall were not raised at Planning Commission.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose annexation and rezoning due to overnight industrial noise/light impacts and uncommitted sidewalk construction.
side_b_arguments: Residential units will sit closer to the FedEx hub than existing neighborhoods, exposing residents to 2–3 a.m. truck noise and lights without a sound wall.
The applicant could not commit to paving or installing pervious surfacing within the 20-foot cemetery pedestrian easement due to uncalculated impervious limits.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and PDR 7.405 rezoning passed 6-1; consistency statement passed 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Shannon at Old Chapel Hill Mixed-Use Rezoning (Item 24)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-1 to approve the Shannon at Old Chapel Hill rezoning, with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman dissenting amid questions about affordable housing proffers and resident traffic/safety objections.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve mixed-use infill density within the Urban Growth Boundary.
side_a_arguments: The Planning Commission recommended approval 12-0 and the site is walkable to retail, dining, the post office, and the Southwest Durham Library.
The developer committed to affordable housing proffers and sidewalk construction linking to MLK.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the rezoning over traffic, pedestrian safety, transit gaps, and affordable housing proffer concerns.
side_b_arguments: Residents warned of severe congestion on a two-lane road, limited sidewalks and public transit, and whether a three-way stop is safe.
Holsey-Hyman specifically questioned the staff report and developer's affordable housing proffers before voting no.
conflicts.resolution: Rezoning passed 5-1; consistency statement passed 6-0.

conflicts.issue: Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association 215-Acre Dedicated Nature Preserve Proposal (Item 7)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-2 on directing staff to engage the state and Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association (ECWA) to pursue Dedicated Nature Preserve (DNP) protection for 215 acres of city-owned property.
conflicts.side_a_position: Direct staff to engage the state and ECWA on dedicating the 215-acre property while adhering to slide 9 boundary and water-infrastructure exclusions.
side_a_arguments: Provides stronger conservation protection for critical watershed areas in partnership with the state and ECWA.
Slide 9 explicitly restricts primary areas to valuable zones, simplifies boundaries, and excludes existing or planned water management infrastructure within 100 feet.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the motion as drafted directing full engagement on the 215-acre DNP dedication.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton stated at 01:54:24 that he could not support the motion as stated.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 4-2; City Manager confirmed staff would engage the state and ECWA on the 215 acres as step one and return to Council.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 22, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Costs, Neighborhood Grade Crossings, and Local Bus Prioritization
conflicts.summary: During the GoTriangle commuter rail feasibility update and RCEP grant support letter poll, council members backed Durham County's federal grant application while raising cost-escalation, East Durham rail-crossing closure, and local bus prioritization concerns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support sending the letter backing Durham County's federal RCEP grant application to study station-area connectivity and East Durham crossing issues.
side_a_arguments: The grant specifically funds feasibility and planning work around crossing closures and corridor equity without committing city construction funds.
Regional commuter rail could move 12,000-18,000 riders daily by 2050 if capital costs and Norfolk Southern negotiations can be managed.
conflicts.side_b_position: Condition support with caution ('sideways thumb') over escalating commuter rail costs versus urgent local bus improvements such as Route 9.
side_b_arguments: Rising commuter rail capital estimates and potential Driver Street/Plum Street crossing closures risk diverting transit attention and funds away from residents relying daily on Route 9 local bus service.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Council gave informal consensus to send the County's RCEP grant support letter while noting local transit priorities.

conflicts.issue: Market-Rate Housing Supply, Public Housing Responsibility, and Environmental Trade-Offs
conflicts.summary: During the five-hour housing retreat, Council divided sharply on whether building market-rate housing prevents displacement, how public housing and low-wage workers are framed, and whether pro-growth annexations compromise water and environmental stewardship.
conflicts.side_a_position: Build supply across all price tiers to absorb high-wealth newcomers, rely on concrete bonds/taxes for subsidies, and view public housing as transitional.
side_a_arguments: Leonardo Williams argued Durham must create higher-end supply so $189,000+ earners do not bid away downtown Black neighborhoods, adding that public housing was meant to be transitional and some people walk off $19/hour jobs.

Mark-Anthony Middleton contended government action only materializes through budgets, bonds ($95M), and dedicated taxes, and pushed back against framing pro-growth votes as 'harm' or 'poisoning water'.
conflicts.side_b_position: Treat housing as a human right, prioritize deep subsidies for low-wage, senior, and disabled residents, and center environmental stewardship in growth decisions.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman pushed back against stigmatizing public housing residents, noting many are elderly, disabled on fixed Social Security, or working multiple low-wage jobs.
DeDreana Freeman and Mayor Elaine O'Neal emphasized protecting tree canopy, water quality, and longtime residents rather than letting private developers dictate Durham's growth pattern.
conflicts.resolution: No formal votes were taken; Council agreed to continue housing deep-dive sessions including a data presentation from DataWorks NC.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 8, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Craig Davis Properties $5M Offer for Durham Center Parking Deck: On-Site Affordable Units and Public Parking Loss
conflicts.summary: Council members diverged sharply in response to Craig Davis Properties' presentation to purchase the Durham Center Parking Deck for $5M and build a 32-story market-rate tower with a $650K off-site housing contribution.
conflicts.side_a_position: Demand on-site affordable housing units and preserve downtown public parking near Carolina Theatre rather than accepting a $650K fund payment.
side_a_arguments: Because the city owns the deck and holds leverage over air-rights changes, Council should require affordable units inside the building itself rather than allowing exclusively luxury $7,000/month three-bedroom apartments downtown.

Reducing 719 city-owned parking spaces directly across from Carolina Theatre and the Convention Center to ~82-84 daytime P1 spaces and 300 evening/weekend spaces weakens city assets and accessibility.
conflicts.side_b_position: Evaluate whether $5M in proceeds, nearly $926K in annual tax revenue, and 308 market-rate units outweigh holding an underperforming parking deck.
side_b_arguments: Adding downtown residential supply absorbs high-income newcomers who otherwise bid up older neighborhood homes and trigger tax-driven displacement.
Middleton argued Council must ask whether the deck currently generates $5M in value and examine residents' quality of life when affordable units sit in high-cost entertainment districts.
conflicts.resolution: Informational presentation only; staff and the developer took Council's feedback back for further negotiation before any formal agenda item.

conflicts.issue: SCAD (TC2200001) Recusal Challenge, Process Legitimacy, and Continuance Timing
conflicts.summary: Debate erupted over whether Javiera Caballero faced a conflict of interest requiring recusal under NCGS 160D-109 and whether delaying SCAD 90 days built public trust or rewarded obstruction ahead of municipal elections.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question potential conflicts of interest in SCAD's drafting and require structured 90-day community engagement with balanced task force oversight before any vote.
side_a_arguments: Emails cited by residents alleged a council member's spouse appeared on early SCAD planning documents, raising questions of inconsistent standards across council members.
Community trust in the planning process and application history had been damaged and required an objective, balanced engagement plan.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject unfounded recusal allegations under NCGS 160D-109, oppose tying land-use decisions to election calendars, and base the eventual SCAD vote on Planning staff's technical analysis.
side_b_arguments: City Attorney Kim Rehberg confirmed NCGS 160D-109 requires a direct, substantial, material financial benefit for recusal, and Javiera Caballero stated her husband had no SCAD involvement.
Tying zoning decisions to upcoming elections ('council shopping') sets a problematic precedent and delays addressing Durham's UDO rewrite and housing needs.
Many public criticisms relied on pre-packaged talking points or mischaracterizations rather than the staff analysis.
conflicts.resolution: Council unanimously granted the applicant's 90-day continuance request to November 20, 2023 while declining to force recusal.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 6, 2022 (audio corrected)
conflicts.issue: Downtown Social District Equity, Open-Container Policing, and Third-Party Contract Complexity
conflicts.summary: While Council generally favored supporting downtown recovery, members debated geographic equity outside downtown, potential disparate open-container enforcement, street closures, and whether Durham's proposed DDI designee contract was overly prescriptive.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move swiftly toward a Downtown Social District with light, streamlined designee agreements modeled on Greensboro to aid small businesses.
side_a_arguments: Downtown businesses are losing post-COVID weekday traffic and competing with Raleigh and Greensboro social districts.
DDI is a trusted city partner, and overly burdensome legal contracts conflict with HB 890's streamlined framework.
Social districts do not contradict equity work any more than balancing unarmed crisis response and ShotSpotter.
conflicts.side_b_position: Address inequities for non-downtown Black business corridors, guard against disparate open-container policing, and explore car-free/transit pairings.
side_b_arguments: Allowing alcohol downtown while people on neighborhood corners elsewhere face open-container enforcement risks creating 'two Durhams'.
City-funded signage and DDI staffing privilege downtown over business districts without paid staff.
Higher-frequency free transit and car-free streeteries should accompany expanded downtown alcohol consumption.
conflicts.resolution: Item 24 was moved to the October 17 General Business Agenda so the City Attorney could address questions regarding the designee contract.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 8, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: ShotSpotter Evaluation Standards and Risk of False-Positive Policing Harm
conflicts.summary: During discussion of pulled Item 27, members clashed over how ShotSpotter's one-year pilot should be evaluated and weighed against potential harms.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support testing ShotSpotter with Duke's Wilson Center external evaluation and judge it on local Durham data, noting even one saved life matters.
side_a_arguments: Durham should not rely on worst-case policing examples from other cities and already evaluates ShotSpotter more rigorously than pilots like Participatory Budgeting.
NCCU Chancellor Akinleye expressed support for technology near campus, and faster Priority-2 alerts can get aid to victims faster.
conflicts.side_b_position: Weigh potential harms—false gunfire alerts, wrongful arrests, and aggressive police responses—equally alongside any potential benefits and scrutinize PB comparisons.
side_b_arguments: Participatory Budgeting is evaluated every cycle and does not carry life-or-liberty policing risks.
If ShotSpotter harms or causes the false imprisonment of one resident, that cost must weigh just as heavily as saving a life.
conflicts.resolution: Javiera Caballero pulled Item 27 from Consent to the September 19 General Business Agenda for a separate vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 18, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Bull City Tenants United Recommendation Requiring Landlords to Maintain Provided Stoves and Refrigerators
conflicts.summary: While backing other Bull City Tenants United proposals, Council split over adding minimum housing-code mandates requiring landlords to keep supplied appliances in working order.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance the housing-code requirement so landlords who provide appliances cannot leave tenants with broken stoves or refrigerators.
side_a_arguments: Working kitchen appliances are basic habitability needs and tenants already pay rents expecting provided appliances to function.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hold or research alternatives rather than enact a mandate that could prompt landlords to stop supplying appliances or raise compliance burdens.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman warned landlords might simply remove appliances from rental units and force tenants to purchase their own.
Leonardo Williams and Mayor Elaine O'Neal questioned NIS code-enforcement capacity and unintended financial consequences for small landlords and tenants.
conflicts.resolution: Separated from the consensus BCTU items (which advanced to the Sept. 6 consent agenda) and referred back to staff for further legal and policy research.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 21, 2023
conflicts.issue: City Council Procedures, Off-Dais Censure Rules, Fraternization Policy, and Handling of Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman Censure Effort
conflicts.summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman clashed sharply with Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton over procedural gaps in council ethics rules, the lack of formal apologies following Holsey-Hyman's exoneration, and allegations of workplace bullying and past physical assault on the dais.
conflicts.side_a_position: Council's rules of procedure contain serious governance gaps on off-dais conduct, citizen complaints, fraternization, and workplace harassment, and members owe closure and apologies to Dr. Holsey-Hyman.
side_a_arguments: Rule 2.14 focuses on dais conduct and lacks clear due-process steps for off-dais allegations, citizen censure requests, or fraternization between council members and senior staff.
After DA and SBI inquiries exonerated Dr. Holsey-Hyman, Council failed to formally close the matter or apologize for attempting to censure her.
DeDreana Freeman alleged ongoing workplace bullying and past physical confrontation by Mark-Anthony Middleton and called for an outside facilitator.
conflicts.side_b_position: No procedural rules were violated during the contemplated censure, citizen petitions do not trigger the Procedures Committee without a council majority, and no apology is owed.
side_b_arguments: Rule 2.14 does not preclude contemplating censure for off-dais conduct, and the resolution was dropped after a private meeting in the interest of healing the city.
The same investigative letter exonerated other council members of collusion, leaving nothing to apologize for.
Mark-Anthony Middleton flatly denied ever hitting DeDreana Freeman and argued any procedural overhaul should wait for the newly elected council.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote or procedural revision was adopted; the dispute remained unresolved at the close of outgoing Mayor Elaine O'Neal's final work session.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 5, 2023
conflicts.issue: Scope of Mid-Year Employee Bonuses and Budget Savings Targets
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether Option 3 sufficiently addressed worker pay demands or whether staff should be pressed to cut an additional $3 million across city budgets to reach a $5,000 bonus goal for employees earning under $90,000.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Option 3 today as a compromise while keeping pressure on staff to identify further savings for the $5,000 target.
side_a_arguments: The adopted budget already assumes $10 million in savings, requiring another $3 million in cuts (totaling $13 million) to reach $5,000.
Option 3 gets funds out quickly while providing higher tiers some relief beyond $500 and focusing more money on lower-paid workers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Push aggressively for departmental, CIP, Participatory Budgeting, or Community Safety reductions to fulfill the full $5,000 ask.
side_b_arguments: Department heads should evaluate 3–5% reductions, CIP slowdowns, or reallocating uncommitted funds to meet the original ask for employees under $90,000.
Option 3 is acceptable as an initial step only with a commitment to continue pursuing the remainder.
conflicts.resolution: Council unanimously adopted Option 3 with an exemption for elected Council members and directed staff to report back on options to cover the additional groupings up to $5,000.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Aug. 24, 2023
conflicts.issue: Creation of an Ad Hoc SCAD Community Engagement Task Force
conflicts.summary: Council clashed over Mayor Elaine O'Neal's proposal to convene an ad hoc SCAD Community Engagement Task Force co-chaired by DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams using volunteers from the August 21 public hearing.
conflicts.side_a_position: Establish a balanced ad hoc task force of SCAD proponents and opponents co-chaired by Freeman and Williams to facilitate public dialogue and restore community trust.
side_a_arguments: Bringing opponents and proponents into the same room can counter misinformation and counterbalance perceived developer influence.
Having two council co-chairs representing differing perspectives would give the public a clear avenue to understand SCAD before a final vote.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject forming an ad hoc task force and rely on professional Planning staff's neutral analysis and standard UDO rewrite engagement.
side_b_arguments: Land use hearings are statutorily prescribed and it is unclear who the task force would report to or what work product it could produce when members already hold entrenched positions.
Past equity task forces used formal application and vetting processes rather than selecting self-selected speakers from one hearing.
Planning staff already provides an unbiased, neutral analysis of SCAD.
conflicts.resolution: Formal task force proposal dropped after lacking majority support (Jillian Johnson departed and Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed); DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams proceeded informally to contact hearing sign-ups.

conflicts.issue: Mayor's Priority Item: Motion to Add ~$8 Million (~2-Cent Property Tax Increase) to Restore Missed FY 2021 Step Raise for City Employees
conflicts.summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal invited an out-of-sequence motion ahead of the budget vote to fund one missed FY 2021 step raise (~$8M via a 2-cent tax hike); the four-member majority voted no, opposing tax hikes prior to a completed pay study.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.issue: Annexation and Rezoning of 901 and 903 Sherron Road: Tree Buffers, Mass Grading, Stormwater Runoff, and Housing Supply
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-2 over annexing and rezoning a 17-acre site at 901 and 903 Sherron Road (Dries Homes Company), balancing adjacent residents' environmental and grading concerns against housing need and project-scale constraints.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 17-acre infill annexation and RS-10(D) rezoning because it provides needed housing and exceeds baseline UDO stormwater requirements.
side_a_arguments: The project exceeds UDO impervious surface limits and provides 100-year storm flood control.
At 17 acres, the parcel is much smaller than 50+ acre developments and cannot realistically proffer large numbers of affordable units or major fund contributions.
Durham continues to need housing supply and incremental improvements over baseline UDO standards.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose approval without stronger protections against mass grading, tree removal, blasting, and runoff onto neighboring properties.
side_b_arguments: Neighbors requested no grading within 10 feet of property lines and a 30-foot wooded buffer at 60% opacity to preserve mature trees.
Residents cited concerns over excavation near property lines, stormwater drainage in buffers, and blasting impacts.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and rezoning ordinances passed 4-2 (Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voting no); the consistency statement subsequently passed 5-1 (DeDreana Freeman voting no).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 23, 2023 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Proposed Censure Resolution Against Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman
conflicts.summary: Council members clashed sharply over both the substance and rapid rollout of a draft censure resolution alleging two incidents involving city staff and political campaign work.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance a formal censure resolution for transparency, ethical accountability, and to protect city staff from chilling effects.
side_a_arguments: A second January 2023 incident established a pattern making the earlier incident seven months prior relevant.
Failing to self-police when staff face discipline sends a chilling message to employees.
Members held one-on-one and partnered meetings beforehand, and Jillian Johnson agreed to edit the draft line regarding whether the second staffer was asked or volunteered.
conflicts.side_b_position: Contest the rushed process, late notice, and factual framing of the censure resolution.
side_b_arguments: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman stated she received the draft at 10:30 PM the night before while traveling without sleep and disputed claims she was adequately consulted.

She maintained she never repeated the first incident after meeting with the City Clerk, and that in the second incident an experienced staffer volunteered after HR clearance and took full HR responsibility.
Other members questioned whether Council was independently determining facts or acting on a predetermined report, and Javiera Caballero urged closing unproductive debate.
conflicts.resolution: No vote was taken; Jillian Johnson agreed to circulate an edited version for consideration at a subsequent meeting before Mayor Elaine O'Neal adjourned the session.

conflicts.issue: Adopt Ordinance Annexing Kemp Road Residential and Authorizing Utility Extension Agreement with Bethesda Association LLC
conflicts.summary: After extended debate over draft growth boundaries east of Kemp Road, fire service coverage, and resident notifications, Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded the annexation and utility extension agreement with Bethesda Association LLC. The clerk closed the vote and reported the motion failed 4-2 (2 ayes, 4 nays), with DeDreana Freeman, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, Jillian Johnson, and Javiera Caballero voting no. City Attorney advice confirmed no jurisdiction remained for the rezoning or consistency statement motions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-4)

conflicts.issue: Geographic Equity and Open-Container Enforcement in the Downtown Social District
conflicts.summary: While all seven Council members ultimately voted 7-0 for the Downtown Social District ordinance, speakers and council members clashed over downtown-focused privileges versus open-container policing risks in lower-income Black neighborhoods.
conflicts.side_a_position: Create the Downtown Social District to match peer NC cities and boost post-pandemic downtown restaurant and retail foot traffic.
side_a_arguments: Nearby cities already run social districts and downtown businesses need economic momentum.
Police Chief Patrice Andrews stated officers focus on violent crime and do not cite simple open containers absent disturbances, and ABC over-service laws still apply.
conflicts.side_b_position: Address geographic exclusivity outside downtown and protect Black residents and Central Park family events from disparate alcohol enforcement and over-policing.
side_b_arguments: Privileging downtown patrons to walk with alcohol while criminalizing open containers in East Durham or neighborhood corners perpetuates 'two Durhams'.
Public drinking zones could overlap with family programming in spaces like Durham Central Park unless boundaries and policing metrics are carefully tracked.
conflicts.resolution: Council passed the ordinance 7-0 while requesting continued oversight of future designee agreements and enforcement equity.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special City Council Meeting: ARPA Funding May 18, 2022 at 2 p.m. (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Selection of ARPA First-Phase Funding Formula (Option B vs. Option C) and Cutoff Equity
conflicts.summary: Council members weighed competing formulas in Council Member Jillian Johnson's ARPA spreadsheet and raised concerns about projects excluded below staff's 24-project cutoff before converging informally on Option C.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support Option C (fund staff 'fund' and 'invite to reapply' projects at 70% up to $1M cap)
side_a_arguments: Broadens funding across both staff-recommended projects and 'invite to reapply' proposals while respecting Council's 50% ARPA spending ceiling
Leaves flexibility for staff scope-of-service negotiations and Treasury compliance review
conflicts.side_b_position: Lean toward Option B (or remain undecided between Option B and Option C)
side_b_arguments: Initial preference expressed by an unnamed speaker leaning toward Option B prior to consensus check, while Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman initially weighed both B and C
conflicts.resolution: Council reached informal consensus on Option C without a formal motion, directing staff to enter scope-of-service contract negotiations up to the capped awards.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting March 23, 2023 10 a.m.
conflicts.issue: City of Durham Mentoring Alliance Collaborative Pilot Program ($200,000 / FTE vs. Referral List or Matching Seed Fund)
conflicts.summary: Council members differed on whether to advance a $200,000 pilot with a dedicated FTE or pursue a smaller, multi-agency coordination model.
conflicts.side_a_position: Establish a City-funded Mentoring Alliance Collaborative pilot to coordinate youth mentoring partners and combat crisis-level youth violence.
side_a_arguments: Youth gun violence demands proactive prevention and a centralized one-stop shop connecting families to mentoring organizations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid committing $200,000 or an FTE that alters Office on Youth workflows before identifying specific gaps; use a simpler directory or a small County/DPS matching seed.
side_b_arguments: Ambiguity remains around where the FTE would sit and whether a referral menu/link from the Office on Youth already achieves a one-stop information hub.
A smaller seed allocation (such as $10,000) could test gaps and invite matching funds from Durham County and Durham Public Schools rather than carrying the full $200,000 cost alone.
conflicts.resolution: Time was called at 00:18:59 for workshop categorization, with discussion of scaling down to a smaller matching seed amount before deciding on an FTE.

conflicts.issue: HEART Team Expansion Framing and Comparisons Between Durham PD and Memphis PD
conflicts.summary: During council announcements, members clashed over how Durham's HEART alternative crisis response expansion and local policing oversight were framed in light of the police killing in Memphis and the tasing death of Darryl Tyree Williams in Raleigh.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advocate expanding the HEART crisis response program to 24/7 citywide coverage in the upcoming budget and highlight alternative response amid national scrutiny of policing.
side_a_arguments: HEART has demonstrated success and should be funded to operate 24/7 across the entire city.

Community rallies with Durham Beyond Policing underscore public demand for non-police crisis response, heightened by national attention following the police killing in Memphis where Durham's former chief serves.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject equating Durham Police Department with Memphis PD, oppose targeting city employees, and invite the Police Chief before Council to address regional incidents.
side_b_arguments: Durham Police Department is not the Memphis Police Department, and policy disputes should be directed at elected officials on the ballot rather than W-2 city employees.
Bringing Durham's Police Chief before Council allows members to ask direct questions about local practices following regional tragedies such as the tasing death of Darryl Tyree Williams in Raleigh.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; DeDreana Freeman seconded Mark-Anthony Middleton's request to bring the Police Chief before Council during the upcoming budget/oversight cycle.

conflicts.issue: East Geer Street Residential Competition for Competitive 9% LIHTC Tax Credits
conflicts.summary: While all seven Council members backed the 90-unit East Geer Street affordable/workforce project, Jillian Johnson and Mark-Anthony Middleton initially expressed concern over whether pursuing competitive 9% tax credits would undermine DHA redevelopment plans.
conflicts.side_a_position: Avoid competing with Durham Housing Authority (DHA) for scarce 9% LIHTC credits unless DHA confirms it has no January 2023 application.
side_a_arguments: Long-standing city-DHA coordination seeks to protect 9% tax credits for public housing redevelopment such as Fayette Place.
conflicts.side_b_position: Zoning should not be conditioned on tax-credit choices, and the applicant committed 25% affordable units even if privately financed.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman viewed linking zoning approval to future 9% credit applications as off-putting, and Leah Bergman noted she checked with Community Development and was happy to build privately if DHA needed the credit.
conflicts.resolution: Jillian Johnson confirmed via text message with DHA CEO Anthony Scott that DHA had no 9% application ready for January 2023, and Council approved all three motions 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Item 17 (Motion 1): Adopt Amended SCAD UDO Text Amendment (TC2200001) Excluding Staff-Unrecommended Sections, Topic 6, and PATH
conflicts.summary: Jillian Johnson moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the SCAD provisions recommended by planning staff while excluding Topic 3 (§6.10.2.A.1), Topic 4 (§4.6.6.C.1, §5.4.2.B.2.a), all of Topic 6, Topic 7 (§6.8.2.A.2.a, §6.8.3, §6.8.4), Topic 8 (§6.10.1.C.1, §6.10.1.D.1, §6.10.2.B.2), Topic 10 (§6.12.3.B.11), Topic 11 (§6.12.5.E), Topic 13 (§6.10.1.C.1.f, §6.10.1.D.1.f), and the Affordable Housing PATH proposal. The motion passed 4-3 by hand vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 17 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Amended SCAD UDO Text Amendment
conflicts.summary: Moved by Leonardo Williams and seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council adopted the statutory consistency statement for the amended SCAD ordinance by the same 4-3 hand vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Perry Farm Consolidated Annexation Ordinance and CSC Group LLC Utility Extension Agreement (Item 24, Motion 1)
conflicts.summary: Annexes Perry Farm into the City of Durham effective Dec. 31, 2023 and authorizes a utility extension agreement with CSC Group LLC.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Perry Farm Zoning Map Change to PDR 3.155 and Rural Residential Public/Civic (Item 24, Motion 2)
conflicts.summary: Transfers property from county Residential Rural (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B) to city Planned Development Residential 3.155 and Rural Residential with a textual development plan limiting uses to public and civic.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 21, 2023
conflicts.issue: Structure and Funding of Mid-Year City Employee Bonuses
conflicts.summary: Council members and staff disagreed over whether to pass the $6.5 million bonus ordinance immediately or delay for reworked tiers that shift more funds to lower earners without cutting part-time bonuses or destabilizing city reserves.
conflicts.side_a_position: Either pass the existing ordinance for immediate early-October payouts or avoid exceeding $6.5M without identified expenditure cuts.
side_a_arguments: Passing the current ordinance allows employees to see money in their first October paycheck.
Finding an extra $4.9M mid-year requires freezing positions or stopping contracts because the budget already assumes a $10M positive variance, and the city cannot jeopardize disaster reserves.
conflicts.side_b_position: Rework the $6.5M allocation (or identify Q2 savings) to increase bonuses for lower-earning workers without reducing part-time worker payouts.
side_b_arguments: The current distribution is unsatisfactory for the lowest-paid employees and higher-tier bonuses can be trimmed closer to the $300 already budgeted.
Part-time employees received only $500 previously and should not have their bonuses reduced.
conflicts.resolution: After a recess, at least six Council members supported deferring the vote and directing staff to bring back reworked bonus options.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 7, 2023
conflicts.issue: City Sanitation and Essential Worker Compensation Adjustments
conflicts.summary: Following protests from sanitation workers over wages and housing affordability, Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton expressed contrasting positions on mid-year pay adjustments versus staying within the adopted budget and compensation study.
conflicts.side_a_position: Stand with protesting workers and pursue immediate budget options to raise compensation.
side_a_arguments: Essential workers face severe inflation and cannot afford to live in Durham while doing vital city work.
Even under statutory balanced-budget rules, Council can identify ways within the numbers to support workers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Rely on the adopted 6% (4% + 2%) pay increase and ongoing compensation study rather than unsustainable mid-year promises.
side_b_arguments: Ad-hoc mid-year raises create recurring obligations that would require raising taxes or cutting services the next year.

conflicts.issue: Hayti Historic Redress Funding Scale and Use of the $30 Million Projected Fund Balance Surplus

conflicts.side_a_position: Put real funding (up to $10 million) on the table for Hayti historic redress without draining the City's rainy-day fund balance.
side_a_arguments: Committing $10 million marks a historic first step that can be supplemented in future budget cycles, CIP updates, and ARPA allocations.
As a self-insured city, Durham cannot raid its entire ~$30 million reserve in one fell swoop without risking fiscal agility.
conflicts.side_b_position: Clarify how the $30 million surplus, ARPA, and CIP align and avoid capping Hayti investment at $10 million without a binding CIP roadmap.
side_b_arguments: If Hayti projects are not placed into the CIP and coordinated with NCDOT, larger transformative investments risk slipping past 2029.
Council should evaluate whether the $30 million surplus can better address department and community priorities alongside ARPA deadlines.
conflicts.resolution: Staff noted green-rated budget priorities totaled $15 million and agreed to return with options balancing ARPA, CIP, fund balance, and general fund sources.

conflicts.issue: Proposed 10-Cent Plastic Bag Fee Ordinance vs. Education-First Resolution
conflicts.summary: Following a presentation by Don't Waste Durham and university clinic researchers, council members divided over whether to advance an enforceable 10-cent plastic bag fee ordinance with a transition period or begin with a non-binding resolution and public education campaign.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support moving forward with a plastic bag fee ordinance paired with a clear timeline and bilingual public education campaign.
side_a_arguments: Pricing undesirable single-use items is a proven tool to drive both individual and collective behavior change.
An ordinance with an explicit transition timeline (such as 18 months) provides clarity while allowing thorough multilingual outreach.
Other jurisdictions worldwide—including countries with much lower average wealth—have successfully implemented plastic bag restrictions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support a robust public education campaign and resolution first, viewing a mandatory 10-cent fee ordinance as premature.
side_b_arguments: A 10-cent per-bag fee creates psychological and financial burdens on low-income residents who already pay more for healthy food.
Policing and enforcing local mandates proved challenging during the pandemic.
A robust education campaign coupled with a resolution can build public buy-in before considering an ordinance.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken at the work session; policy discussion left open for further council work.

conflicts.side_a_position: Implement the proposed 6%-8% base-pay increases (7% for public safety) while completing the pay study before adding unallocated funds, leaving retroactive raises open for consideration.
side_a_arguments: Higher taxes disproportionately burden lowest-income residents.
Adding unallocated money without a finalized plan is fiscally irresponsible.
The proposed budget already includes a 2% step plus 5% pay plan increase (7% total) added permanently to base pay for public safety staff.
conflicts.side_b_position: Explore reallocating $7 million to $8 million within the budget or raising taxes to protect employee morale and address public safety compensation sooner.
side_b_arguments: Public safety and city worker morale are suffering from salary compression and regional competition.
The city could examine finding $7M-$8M across the broader budget or consider a tax increase, though acknowledging four votes for a tax hike were unlikely.

conflicts.issue: Role of Public Housing vs. Mixed-Income Private-Market Partnerships
conflicts.summary: During the Durham Housing Authority deep-dive discussion, council members diverged on whether concentrated public housing is a failed model that must shift toward mixed-income communities or whether government-funded public housing must be championed as a guaranteed human right.
conflicts.side_a_position: Shift away from concentrated public housing toward structured mixed-income communities that integrate residents socioeconomically rather than isolating low-income households.
side_a_arguments: Concentrated public housing can trap residents in environments with maintenance failures and crime.
Mixed-income communities create better-run, welcoming environments that encourage upward mobility and integration into Durham.
conflicts.side_b_position: Government-funded public housing is 100% the solution and housing must be treated and funded as a guaranteed human right rather than left to a capitalist market.
side_b_arguments: Public housing only struggles when the federal government underfunds it, unlike systems in Western Europe where government investment keeps housing affordable.
Treating housing purely as a market commodity guarantees displacement and homelessness for residents who cannot pay market rates.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 21, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: In outgoing Mayor Elaine O'Neal's final work session on November 21, 2023 (with Jillian Johnson excused), Council heard three major presentations: the 2023 Third Quarter Crime Report (showing homicides up 9.4% to 45 and motor vehicle thefts up 156%, alongside an 80% homicide clearance rate and 24.7% police vacancy rate), the Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Initiative core team update on housing barriers for justice-involved individuals, and the FY 2023-24 First Quarter Financial Report. The session concluded with an explosive, nearly hour-long confrontation under Item 6 (City Council Procedures) over censure gaps, fraternization policy, the aborted March 2023 censure of Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and mutual accusations of dishonesty, bullying, and past physical altercation between DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton. Council unanimously settled the December 4 agenda (6-0) before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Carver Creek & Wheels Comments, and Citizen Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the meeting to order at 1:00 PM with Jillian Johnson excused. Mark-Anthony Middleton noted the County's guaranteed income documentary screening, speakers praised Carver Creek's anti-displacement preservation and urged ADA/roller-derby design attention at the former Wheels Skating Center, and solid waste worker speakers celebrated solidarity, while Dennis Garrett urged holiday youth crime prevention.

agenda_items.title: 2023 Third Quarter Crime Report Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Patrice Andrews reported overall Part 1 violent crime down 5.5% (612 per 100,000), with homicides up 9.4% to 45 (80% clearance rate) and rapes up 21.6% driven by prior-year reports, while robberies fell 21.3%. Property crime surged, led by a 156% jump in motor vehicle thefts (largely Hyundais and Kias) and 837 seized guns; ShotSpotter logged 1,125 alerts (26.3% with 911 calls), and sworn staffing stood at 77% (24.7% vacancy rate).

agenda_items.title: Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Initiative Core Team Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carmisha Wallace, Colin Davis, and community partner Dennis Garrett presented findings from nine months of Bloomberg Harvard coaching and interviews with justice-involved individuals, landlords, and service providers. They recommended a coordinated 'one-stop shop' entry system, peer support specialists, and landlord engagement, noting Bloomberg awarded 20 additional coaching hours that incoming Mayor Leonardo Williams committed to continuing.

agenda_items.title: FY 2023-2024 First Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Management Services Director Christina Reardon presented Q1 financial results, noting property tax revenues appeared 89% lower than Q1 FY23 only because tax bills mailed later, while occupancy tax rose nearly 40%, sales tax stood around $13M for two months, and inspections fund personnel remained under budget due to vacancies. DeDreana Freeman asked staff to highlight red-flagged CIP projects early to avoid re-bidding cost escalation.

agenda_items.title: Discussion of City Council Procedures, Censure Process, and Fraternization Gaps
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal presented a City Attorney-commissioned 23-page review identifying gaps in council rules regarding off-dais conduct, citizen censure petitions, fraternization, and lack of apologies/closure after Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's exoneration. Mark-Anthony Middleton countered that Rule 2.14 did not violate procedures, no apology was owed for a censure dropped at a private community meeting, and accused O'Neal and others of echoing activist talking points; heated exchanges followed between DeDreana Freeman, Middleton, and Holsey-Hyman.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations and Settling of December 4 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported a council tie on Item 1 (Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee) between re-advertising and nominating Hannah Bartlebaugh, leaving it for re-advertisement. Council unanimously approved placing Items 1-5 and 7-21 on Consent and Items 24-26 on Public Hearings before Mayor O'Neal closed her final work session with pointed parting remarks to Mark-Anthony Middleton.

votes.notes: Jillian Johnson had an excused absence.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Mark-Anthony Middleton and seconded by Javiera Caballero, Council unanimously approved the agenda for the December 4 regular meeting among the six members present, omitting pulled Item 6 (City Council Procedures).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 21, 2023
disagreements.issue: City Council Procedures, Off-Dais Censure Rules, Fraternization Policy, and Handling of Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman Censure Effort
disagreements.summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman clashed sharply with Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton over procedural gaps in council ethics rules, the lack of formal apologies following Holsey-Hyman's exoneration, and allegations of workplace bullying and past physical assault on the dais.
disagreements.side_a_position: Council's rules of procedure contain serious governance gaps on off-dais conduct, citizen complaints, fraternization, and workplace harassment, and members owe closure and apologies to Dr. Holsey-Hyman.
side_a_arguments: Rule 2.14 focuses on dais conduct and lacks clear due-process steps for off-dais allegations, citizen censure requests, or fraternization between council members and senior staff.
After DA and SBI inquiries exonerated Dr. Holsey-Hyman, Council failed to formally close the matter or apologize for attempting to censure her.
DeDreana Freeman alleged ongoing workplace bullying and past physical confrontation by Mark-Anthony Middleton and called for an outside facilitator.
disagreements.side_b_position: No procedural rules were violated during the contemplated censure, citizen petitions do not trigger the Procedures Committee without a council majority, and no apology is owed.
side_b_arguments: Rule 2.14 does not preclude contemplating censure for off-dais conduct, and the resolution was dropped after a private meeting in the interest of healing the city.
The same investigative letter exonerated other council members of collusion, leaving nothing to apologize for.
Mark-Anthony Middleton flatly denied ever hitting DeDreana Freeman and argued any procedural overhaul should wait for the newly elected council.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote or procedural revision was adopted; the dispute remained unresolved at the close of outgoing Mayor Elaine O'Neal's final work session.
