meetings.title: City Council Budget Work Session May 24, 2023 at 9:00 am
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 24, 2023 Budget Work Session (Day 1), Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton opened the meeting and called a brief five-minute recess until Mayor Elaine O'Neal arrived to assume the chair, and Middleton later gaveled out at 12:35 p.m. City Manager Wanda Page introduced new Solid Waste Director James Lyons and joined council members in honoring the budget team's work following the passing of the late Budget Director. Budget staff presented the refreshed FY 2024-2026 Strategic Plan (organized around five goals and 41 tracked initiatives) and began reviewing General Fund revenues, where property tax (47%) and sales tax (35%) represent the largest sources. After an omitted middle segment, General Services presented its ~$18.5 million budget (including new City Hall and facility physical security positions/contracts and Cultural Roadmap work) and Durham Parks and Recreation presented a largely flat budget featuring ~$100,000 for operating the Wheels Roller Skating Rink.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Staff Introductions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton opened the session and took a five-minute recess until Mayor Elaine O'Neal arrived at 00:06:27, with roll call noting O'Neal, Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman present and DeDreana Freeman arriving later. Speakers thanked Interim Budget Director Christina Reardon and budget staff, and City Manager Wanda Page introduced new Solid Waste Director James Lyons.

agenda_items.title: FY 2024-2026 Strategic Plan Refresh Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sherry Metcalf of the Budget Department presented the final refreshed Strategic Plan scheduled for June adoption alongside the budget, distilling citywide priorities into five goals and 41 prioritized initiatives tracked through D-Stat meetings. Highlighted initiatives included expanding WORKS workforce programming in OEWD, affordable housing and hiring a Digital Inclusion Manager in Technology Solutions, and recruitment, retention, and equity efforts.

agenda_items.title: General Fund Revenue Overview (Opening)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Budget Director Christina Reardon began presenting the General Fund revenue picture, highlighting that property taxes (47%) and sales taxes (35%) constitute the primary revenue streams supporting city operations.

agenda_items.title: General Services Department FY 2024 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle segment, General Services leadership (including Assistant Director Stacey Poston) reviewed the department's ~$18.5 million budget (largely personnel and operating, with ~$602k in cemetery revenue and $27k from Durham County for Keep Durham Beautiful). Updates included an 8-day average reactive maintenance turnaround, natural burial ordinance revisions coming after the break, Cultural Roadmap completion by June 2024, and recommended funding for a Physical Security Specialist and contracted courtesy/security officers for City Hall weapons detection, parking garages, and DPR facilities.

agenda_items.title: Durham Parks and Recreation (DPR) FY 2024 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPR presented a generally flat FY 2024 operating budget, with the main capital/other increase driven by approximately $100,000 toward operating the Wheels Roller Skating Rink while design improvements and vendor contract negotiations proceed, alongside discussion of MyDurham teen programming and pool maintenance challenges.

agenda_items.title: Closing Remarks on Budget Season
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and City Manager Wanda Page commended city staff and paid tribute to the late Budget Director ahead of the June 5 public hearing and the next day's budget work session, before Middleton gaveled the session closed at 12:35 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session May 18, 2023 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 18, 2023 Work Session, all seven council members were present at the outset (with DeDreana Freeman announcing she would depart early around 2:00 p.m.). During announcements, Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton previewed a forthcoming Durham-tailored resolution adopting the IHRA definition of anti-Semitism following a meeting with a local rabbi and the Anti-Defamation League. Council unanimously approved City Manager Wanda Page's priority items (including the 2023 Q1 Crime Report, Durham County Transit Plan participation agreement, and Carver Creek Supportive Housing Acquisition) by a 7-0 voice vote. After an omitted middle section, Finance staff presented the FY 2023 Third Quarter financial report showing a projected $9.8 million General Fund expenditure savings and $11.1 million revenue surplus (led by sales tax), and Council settled the next regular meeting agenda by unanimous voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Forthcoming Anti-Semitism Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Leonardo Williams praised the SwingPals youth golf program at Lowes Grove and Hillandale; DeDreana Freeman reflected on Bike Durham's Ride of Silence and noted her 2:00 p.m. early departure; Mayor Elaine O'Neal commended Water Management staff after touring facilities and noted May 24 schedule conflicts. Mark-Anthony Middleton recognized Older Americans, Mental Health Awareness, AAPI, and Jewish American Heritage months, announcing plans to bring forward a Durham-tailored resolution adopting the IHRA definition of anti-Semitism alongside his upcoming hip-hop resolution.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items (Items 21, 28, and 33)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented three priority items: Item 21 (2023 First Quarter Crime Report, 20-minute presentation), Item 28 (Durham County Transit Plan Comprehensive Participation Agreement, adding attachment 2), and Item 33 (Carver Creek Supportive Housing Acquisition, adding attachments 6-14, 30-minute presentation). Moved by Leonardo Williams and seconded by Javiera Caballero, the priority items passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: FY 2023 Third Quarter Financial Projections
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle segment, Finance staff (Mr. Floyd) reported projected FY 2023 General Fund spending of $265.7M against a $275.5M budget (~$9.8M under budget, driven by $7.5M in vacancy savings) and revenues of $259.1M vs. $248M budgeted (+$11.1M, driven by $97.5M projected sales tax and $938k over budget in occupancy tax). Across enterprise funds, Water & Sewer (+$1.8M), Transit (+$2.5M due to driver shortages), Stormwater (+$341k), and DPAC (+$1.1M) showed positive variances, while Solid Waste required a fund balance budget amendment for fuel and overtime/temp costs and Parking saw +$614k revenue growth despite remaining in a cash deficit.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Nominations Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk read council nominations for the Citizen Advisory Committee (Alicia Curry, Laura Girard), Workforce Development Board (Julie A. Pack), Durham Open Space and Trails Commission (Shakira Campbell, Stephen A. Cohen, Melissa Souther), Environmental Affairs Board (Julie Ann Malavade), Human Relations Commission (John J. Hoffman), Durham Sports Commission (Angelique Stallings), and Durham Cultural Advisory Board (Margaret E. McNabb).

agenda_items.title: Motion to Settle the Next Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page recommended placing Items 1-32 on Consent and Items 36-40 on GBA Public Hearings. Moved by Javiera Caballero and seconded by Leonardo Williams, the motion carried unanimously prior to adjournment at 4:50 p.m.

Moved by Leonardo Williams and seconded by Javiera Caballero, the motion passed unanimously.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 15, 2023 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: The May 15, 2023 regular City Council meeting ran until 12:34 a.m. on May 16, beginning with a Period Supplies Awareness proclamation, council announcements (including plans for a 50th anniversary of hip-hop resolution and youth gun violence remarks), and reading of the Consent and General Business Agendas (which included the FY 2023-24 proposed budget presentation and GoDurham transit contracts). Following an omitted middle portion of the transcript digest, Council concluded a contested public hearing on a 17-acre annexation and rezoning at 901 and 903 Sherron Road by Dries Homes Company, where neighbors and DeDreana Freeman raised tree preservation, mass grading, blasting, and stormwater runoff concerns while proponents argued the project exceeded UDO stormwater standards and added needed housing. Council passed the annexation and rezoning ordinances 4-2 (with Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman dissenting) and the consistency statement 5-1 (Freeman dissenting). Finally, Council held a public hearing and unanimously adopted an ordinance increasing FY 2024 stormwater rates (Item 31) effective July 1, 2023.

agenda_items.title: Period Supplies Awareness Proclamation and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal read a Period Supplies Awareness proclamation, and Public Works staff were recognized ahead of National Public Works Week and the May 25 equipment rodeo. DeDreana Freeman spoke on youth gun violence trauma following a Remembrance Day event organized with school board member Jovonia Lewis, Mark-Anthony Middleton announced an upcoming resolution celebrating the 50th anniversary of hip-hop ahead of Bimbé, and Leonardo Williams highlighted youth programs SwingPals, Sidekicks Academy, and Project 300.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items and Reading of Consent and General Business Agendas
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented priority updates for Item 24 (FY 2023-24 Proposed Budget and FY 2024-29 CIP presentation) and Item 28 (Consolidated Annexation – Carpenter Preserve, updating cost-benefit analysis from 235 to 260 units). Mayor Elaine O'Neal read the Consent Agenda (Items 1-3, 5-23, covering board appointments, Commerce Street Apartments housing revenue bonds, street/bridge contracts, GoDurham Access and Fixed Route RATP Dev transit contracts, and DCHC MPO transition to TJCOG) and General Business Agenda items including Harlow Point (Item 27) and Carpenter Preserve (Item 28).

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Zoning Map Change: 901 and 903 Sherron Road (Dries Homes Company)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle segment, residents and DeDreana Freeman pressed the applicant (Dries Homes Company) on mass grading, tree preservation (requesting no grading within 10 feet of property lines and a 30-foot wooded buffer), stormwater runoff, and blasting impacts around the 17-acre infill parcel. Proponents argued the project exceeded UDO impervious surface and 100-year stormwater standards and that 17-acre parcels lack capacity for large affordable housing proffers. Council approved the annexation and utility agreement 4-2, the RS-10(D) Falls/Jordan District B rezoning 4-2 (Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voting no on both), and the NCGS consistency statement 5-1 (Freeman voting no).

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Ordinance: FY 2024 Stormwater Rates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Paul Wiebke (Public Works) presented FY 2024 stormwater fee increases effective July 1, 2023: Tier 1 residential increasing by $0.75 to $4.95/month, Tier 2 by $1.55 to $10.25/month, Tier 3 by $3.11 to $20.53/month, and other residential/non-residential by $1.55 per 2,400 sq. ft. of impervious surface ($10.25/month). No public speakers commented during the hearing, and Council unanimously adopted the revised fee schedule before adjourning at 12:34 a.m. on May 16.

votes.item_title: Adopt Annexation Ordinance for 901 and 903 Sherron Road (Effective June 30, 2023) and Authorize Utility Agreement with Dries Homes Company
votes.notes: Six members voted at 12:30 a.m.; Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Leonardo Williams seconded in favor, joined by two additional affirmative votes (among Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, one of whom was absent/not voting).
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted 4-2 to annex 901 and 903 Sherron Road into the City of Durham effective June 30, 2023 and authorize a utility extension agreement with Dries Homes Company, over objections from Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman regarding tree buffers, mass grading, and stormwater runoff.

votes.item_title: Adopt Zoning Map Change Ordinance for 901 and 903 Sherron Road (RR / RS-20 F/J-B to RS-10(D) F/J-B)
votes.notes: Six members voted; Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voted no, while four members voted aye (mover Mark-Anthony Middleton, seconder Leonardo Williams, and two other members).
votes.discussion_detail: On a motion by Mark-Anthony Middleton and second by Leonardo Williams, Council voted 4-2 to rezone 901 and 903 Sherron Road from Rural Residential and RS-20 (Falls/Jordan District B) county jurisdiction to RS-10(D) with a textual development plan in city jurisdiction.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605) for 901 and 903 Sherron Road Rezoning
votes.notes: Six members voted; DeDreana Freeman voted no, and Mayor Elaine O'Neal joined the majority on the consistency statement alongside mover Mark-Anthony Middleton, seconder Leonardo Williams, and two other members.
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved the statutory consistency statement for the 901 and 903 Sherron Road rezoning by a 5-1 vote, with DeDreana Freeman casting the sole dissenting vote.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Adopt Ordinance Amending Fee Schedule to Revise FY 2024 Stormwater Rates (Effective July 1, 2023)
votes.notes: Clerk announced 'The motion is unanimous' with six members present at 12:33 a.m. (Jillian Johnson and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman: one present voting aye and one absent earlier during the 4-2/5-1 votes).
votes.discussion_detail: Following a public hearing with no speakers, Council unanimously adopted the ordinance raising monthly residential and non-residential stormwater rates effective July 1, 2023 on a motion by Javiera Caballero, seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton.

disagreements.issue: Annexation and Rezoning of 901 and 903 Sherron Road: Tree Buffers, Mass Grading, Stormwater Runoff, and Housing Supply
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-2 over annexing and rezoning a 17-acre site at 901 and 903 Sherron Road (Dries Homes Company), balancing adjacent residents' environmental and grading concerns against housing need and project-scale constraints.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 17-acre infill annexation and RS-10(D) rezoning because it provides needed housing and exceeds baseline UDO stormwater requirements.
side_a_arguments: The project exceeds UDO impervious surface limits and provides 100-year storm flood control.
At 17 acres, the parcel is much smaller than 50+ acre developments and cannot realistically proffer large numbers of affordable units or major fund contributions.
Durham continues to need housing supply and incremental improvements over baseline UDO standards.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose approval without stronger protections against mass grading, tree removal, blasting, and runoff onto neighboring properties.
side_b_arguments: Neighbors requested no grading within 10 feet of property lines and a 30-foot wooded buffer at 60% opacity to preserve mature trees.
Residents cited concerns over excavation near property lines, stormwater drainage in buffers, and blasting impacts.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning ordinances passed 4-2 (Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voting no); the consistency statement subsequently passed 5-1 (DeDreana Freeman voting no).

meetings.title: City Council Subcommittee with Durham Association of Realtors - May 11, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The May 11, 2023 City Council Subcommittee meeting with the Durham Association of Realtors focused on expanding homeownership pathways and reducing financing barriers for Durham residents, with Mayor Elaine O'Neal joining at 00:23:59 while a council subcommittee chair facilitated the session. Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented the City's revised Down Payment Assistance (DPA) program—offering up to $80,000 as a 15-year interest-free forgivable second mortgage starting July 2023—where borrowers apply first through participating primary lenders before City review. Members also discussed FHA policy shifts allowing 30% of Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) income for qualification, preserving Forever Home Durham ADU pilot funds for long-term homeowners, and appraisal gaps caused by cash buyers. Durham Housing Authority staff then presented the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) Homeownership Program, detailing eligibility rules, Housing Quality Standards inspections, and counseling partnerships before members set a tentative June 8 follow-up date and adjourned.

agenda_items.title: Subcommittee Opening and Attendance Check
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Participants convened virtually and checked attendance, noting that DeDreana Freeman and Mayor Elaine O'Neal had not yet joined; staff agreed to reach out while the subcommittee proceeded with the agenda. Mayor O'Neal joined the meeting at 00:23:59.

agenda_items.title: City Down Payment Assistance (DPA) Program Guidelines and Lender Workflow
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented the redesigned Down Payment Assistance program, providing up to $80,000 as a 15-year interest-free forgivable second mortgage for primary residences within Durham (layerable with NCHFA first-time homebuyer funds). Johnson explained that a June 2023 lender workshop would establish participating lenders ahead of a July 2023 launch, and that borrowers will apply directly to a first-mortgage lender for initial underwriting before the City evaluates eligibility for the second mortgage.

agenda_items.title: Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), Forever Home Durham Pilot Funds, and Appraisal Challenges
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Realtor participants reported that FHA would begin counting 30% of ADU income toward borrower qualification (noting due-on-sale clause hurdles), while council participants asked whether ADU pilot funds under the ~$160 million five-year Forever Home Durham program would remain dedicated to helping established long-term homeowners. City Manager Wanda Page confirmed the administration still planned to deliver all originally communicated Forever Home Durham components. Participants also discussed appraisal challenges when cash investors outbid program buyers on $180,000-$300,000 homes needing repairs.

agenda_items.title: Durham Housing Authority Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) Homeownership Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DHA staff briefed the subcommittee on the HCV Homeownership Program, which applies a 70%/30% subsidy structure toward mortgage payments instead of rent for eligible Durham residents employed full-time (30+ hours/week) with no current homeownership. Staff explained pre-purchase Housing Quality Standards (HQS) inspections and noted that while DHA ended its internal HUD counseling program, it partners with Habitat and other organizations and can look into adding counseling options.

agenda_items.title: Scheduling Next Subcommittee Meeting and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Subcommittee members discussed adopting a recurring second-Thursday schedule (targeting June 8, pending a scheduling poll around potential budget work sessions and inviting landlord representatives). Mayor Elaine O'Neal offered closing remarks emphasizing support for vulnerable residents before the meeting adjourned.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session May 4, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 4, 2023 work session (with Javiera Caballero on excused absence), the Durham City Council approved City Manager priority items and scheduled a closed session for two litigation matters. Council heard public comments from pickleball advocates requesting FY 2024 funding for Piney Wood Park court renovations, evening lighting, and winterized restrooms. Staff presented an informational briefing on the 751 South consolidated annexation and Utility Extension Agreement (UEA) options ahead of the upcoming public hearing, as well as proposed FY 2024 stormwater rates supporting over $22 million in capital outlay. Council settled the May 15 regular meeting agenda and granted informal consensus for Jillian Johnson to bring an expedited draft resolution opposing expected North Carolina General Assembly abortion restrictions outside the standard two-work-session review cycle before adjourning to closed session.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Attorney Priority Items and Closed Session Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented priority items including presentations on the UNRBA FY 2024 budget (Item 13), proposed FY 2023-24 water and sewer rates (Item 22), FY 2024 stormwater rates (Item 31), the May 15 budget and CIP presentation schedule (Item 24), and the addition of a deed-for-donation form (Appendix D) to Attachment G for 751 South (Items 26 and 29). City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg requested a closed session at the conclusion of regular business under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation on two lawsuits against the City.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Reading and Pulled Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal read the draft agenda into the record, covering board appointments, Commerce Street Apartments multifamily housing revenue bonds, American Dance Festival grant funding, public works street and bridge contracts, GoDurham Access and fixed-route transit contracts, and the Harlow Point and Carpenter Preserve annexations. Council members pulled Item 4 (minutes), Item 7 (Dixie Lawn Service I-85 median maintenance), Item 17 (GoDurham Access assignment), and Item 18 (GoDurham fixed-route contract with RATP Dev USA) for separate discussion.

agenda_items.title: Piney Wood Park Pickleball Facilities and Budget Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents including Heidi Wilson thanked Council for prior support and asked the City to allocate FY 2024 budget funds to complete stalled pickleball court renovations at Piney Wood Park. Speakers also urged funding to turn on newly installed evening court lights and upgrade restrooms for year-round winterized access to support recreational and tournament play.

agenda_items.title: 751 South Informational Item and Utility Extension Agreement Options
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff outlined Council's upcoming decision on 751 South following state legislative annexation action, explaining the choice between approving an amended Utility Extension Agreement (UEA2) or keeping recorded UEA1 in effect alongside mandatory translational zoning (Mixed Use with Development Plan and Residential Rural) within 60 days. UEA1 commits to up to 1,300 residential units, office floor space, widening NC-751 to four lanes from the southern property line to Stagecoach Road and Renaissance Parkway, and donating 10.5 acres for an elementary school or 22.5 acres for an elementary/middle campus to Durham Public Schools. Staff confirmed that additional developer proffers could still be negotiated up through the public hearing.

agenda_items.title: FY 2024 Proposed Stormwater Rates Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff presented the FY 2024 stormwater rate model, reporting an early April NPDES permit renewal filing and projecting over $22 million in FY 2024 capital outlay and nearly $21.5 million in FY 2025. Staff reviewed customer tiers including over 9,600 Tier 3 residential accounts and approximately 6,454 commercial accounts subject to ERU rates, while a Council member highlighted that residents may pay stormwater charges in monthly installments rather than a single annual bill. One Council member departed at 03:04:49 prior to the closed session.

agenda_items.title: Settling the May 15, 2023 City Council Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page recommended placing Items 1-3 and 5-23 on the Consent Agenda, Items 4 and 24 on the General Business Agenda (GBA), and Items 27-31 on GBA Public Hearings for the May 15 meeting.

agenda_items.title: March 6 Censure Minutes Clarification and Expedited Reproductive Rights Resolution Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman thanked DeDreana Freeman for addressing written documentation in the March 6 minutes regarding the censure resolution. Jillian Johnson asked colleagues for an expedited waiver of the two-work-session resolution policy so Council could respond rapidly if the North Carolina General Assembly enacted a 12-week abortion ban; colleagues gave informal thumbs-up consensus contingent on reviewing the draft language by email prior to adjournment into closed session.

votes.item_title: Approval of City Manager's Priority Items
votes.notes: Javiera Caballero had an excused absence.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page added presentations and Attachment G deed-for-donation updates for Items 13, 22, 24, 26, 29, and 31. DeDreana Freeman moved approval and Leonardo Williams seconded; Mayor Elaine O'Neal called for a show of left hands and declared the motion passed unanimously.

votes.notes: Javiera Caballero had an excused absence.
votes.discussion_detail: Pursuant to NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3), the City Attorney requested a closed session for attorney-client consultation regarding settlement/handling of two cases (20 CVS 265 in Durham County Superior Court and Darryl Daugherty v. City of Durham, 23 CV 133 in federal Middle District). Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded; the motion passed unanimously by show of hands.

votes.discussion_detail: Following the closed-session vote, Mayor Elaine O'Neal called a separate vote to formally approve the City Attorney's priority item list. Stated as moved and properly seconded in the transcript, the motion passed unanimously by show of left hands.

votes.item_title: Settle the May 15, 2023 City Council Agenda
votes.notes: One unnamed Council member announced leaving early at 03:04:49 and would miss closed session; Javiera Caballero was absent.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page assigned Items 1-3 and 5-23 to Consent, Items 4 and 24 to GBA, and Items 27-31 to GBA Public Hearings. Leonardo Williams moved to settle the agenda and Jillian Johnson seconded; the motion passed unanimously by show of hands with no opposition.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 1, 2023 [Live stream]
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 1, 2023 regular meeting (with Javiera Caballero on excused absence), the Durham City Council presented four ceremonial proclamations including Excelsior Hook and Ladder Company Day, Lupus Awareness Month, Black Maternal Health Awareness Month, and Humility Month. Council approved the Consent Agenda 6-0, adopting the Naming Rights Policy for public facilities, the Day of Remembrance resolution, the McKissick Square ARPA affordable housing loan commitment, and the NCDOT Cornwallis Road grade separation agreement. On the sole split vote of the night, Council voted 4-2 (with Mark-Anthony Middleton and Jillian Johnson opposed) to direct staff to engage the state and Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association (ECWA) on dedicating 215 acres into the state Dedicated Nature Preserve program. Council also held a public hearing and voted 6-0 across five motions to adopt the FY 2023-24 Annual Action Plan and HUD grant project ordinances for CDBG, HOME, ESG, and HOPWA.

agenda_items.title: May 2023 Ceremonial Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members read four proclamations honoring the historic Excelsior Hook and Ladder Company (DeDreana Freeman, with a commemorative plaque presented later at 02:16:02), Lupus Awareness Month (Leonardo Williams), Black Maternal Health Awareness Month (Jillian Johnson), and Humility Month (Elaine O'Neal).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Including Naming Rights Policy, McKissick Square ARPA Loan, and Day of Remembrance Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page noted revisions to Item 7 (Attachment 3) and Item 15 (adding a name revocation process to the naming rights policy). Council approved the Consent Agenda, encompassing CASA Bryant Place Apartments loan amendments, waste transfer station contract amendments, the NCDOT Cornwallis Road grade separation agreement (TIP P-5717), the Day of Remembrance resolution, the naming rights policy, the McKissick Square ARPA affordable housing loan commitment, and benefits consulting services.

agenda_items.title: Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association (ECWA) Dedicated Nature Preserve Proposal Alternatives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services staff (David Fleischer) presented responses to Councilwoman Caballero's questions confirming an 800-foot southern corridor carve-out for the future Northern Durham Parkway and outlining combinations of state Dedicated Nature Preserve (DNP) and Registered Heritage Area protections. ECWA representatives supported permanent conservation while expressing appreciation for staff collaboration. Following extended debate, Council voted 4-2 to direct staff to engage the state and ECWA on dedicating the 215-acre property identified in the presentation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-2 (Mark-Anthony Middleton and Jillian Johnson opposed)

agenda_items.title: FY 2023-2024 Annual Action Plan Public Hearing and HUD Grant Project Ordinances
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff (Colin Davis) presented the FY 2023-24 Annual Action Plan for HUD submission by May 15, covering anticipated federal formula allocations across CDBG, HOME, ESG, and HOPWA. No speakers signed up in person or virtually, and after closing the public hearing Council adopted the Annual Action Plan and four corresponding grant project ordinances.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session April 20, 2023 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Elaine O'Neal, Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Javiera Caballero on excused absences, Presiding Chair Jillian Johnson convened a bare-quorum four-member work session on April 20, 2023. Council approved priority items—including referring the SCAD UDO text amendment back to City-County Planning and adding supplemental items on public naming rights, McKissick Square ARPA funding, and benefits consulting—and authorized a closed session regarding Wake County RDU Airport Authority litigation. Old Farm neighborhood residents and former Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden voiced environmental health, benzene, and traffic safety concerns regarding the new Northern High School project. Staff presented options for the Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association 215-acre preserve (recommending Registered Heritage Area status plus a city code ordinance over state Dedicated Nature Preserve restrictions) and briefed Council on the proposed Naming Rights Policy before Council settled the May 1 agenda and entered closed session.

agenda_items.title: City Manager, City Attorney, and Clerk Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page added a 15-minute presentation for Item 7 (ECWA preserve alternatives), referred Item 12 (SCAD UDO text amendment) back to City-County Planning, and added supplemental Items 15 (Naming Rights Policy), 16 (McKissick Square development loan commitment), and 17 (Benefits consulting contract). City Attorney requested a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) regarding two Wake County cases (DOT v. Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority, 18 CVS 1932 and 18 CVS 3817), and the Clerk noted revisions to the Day of Remembrance resolution (Item 14).

agenda_items.title: Agenda Reading and Old Farm Neighborhood Concerns Over New Northern High School
agenda_items.discussion_summary: During citizens' matters, former Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden and neighborhood speakers read a letter from Mary Vickers raising serious health, benzene exposure, senior resident, and traffic-access concerns for the 1,000+ residents of Old Farm near the proposed New Northern High School site and Old Well Street, and criticizing the Board of Adjustment process.

agenda_items.title: Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association (ECWA) Dedicated Nature Preserve Alternatives Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services staff compared the state Dedicated Nature Preserve (DNP) program against the state Registered Heritage Area program for the city-owned parcel, noting an 800-foot carve-out for the future Northern Durham Parkway and restrictions around a closed landfill site requiring gas probes and monitoring. Staff recommended Registered Heritage Area registration paired with a self-directed city code amendment (modeled on Little River and Lake Michie) rather than full DNP dedication requiring Governor and Council of State approval to modify, whereas ECWA favored permanent conservation. Due to three Council absences, members moved Item 7 to the May 1 General Business Agenda for full Council debate.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Placed on May 1 GBA without vote

agenda_items.title: Resolution and Policy for Naming Rights of Publicly Owned Properties and Facilities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Responding to Chair Jillian Johnson's question on why the policy was being introduced now, Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson explained that inquiries routed via Durham County revealed the City lacked a formal naming rights policy; staff benchmarked Durham County's 2016 policy and Raleigh's policy and included a name revocation procedure.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Settlement, Gun Violence Resolution, and Personal Privilege Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page set the May 1 Consent Agenda (Items 1-6, 8-10, 14-17), GBA (Item 7), and GBA Public Hearings (Item 11). Under Other Matters, DeDreana Freeman thanked colleagues for advancing the gun violence Day of Remembrance resolution for May 1, and Leonardo Williams urged the public for grace while rejecting rumors that Council members were sleeping during moments of silence or had pre-judged SCAD prior to its hearing.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Agenda settlement and closed-session motions passed 4-0

votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously approved holding a closed session after regular business under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) regarding Wake County litigation DOT v. Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority et al. (18 CVS 1932 and 18 CVS 3817).

votes.notes: Elaine O'Neal, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Javiera Caballero had excused absences.
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously settled the May 1 agenda as recommended by City Manager Wanda Page, placing Item 7 (ECWA) on GBA, Item 11 on GBA Public Hearings, and all other items on Consent.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting April 17, 2023 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the April 17, 2023 regular meeting (with Javiera Caballero absent), Mayor Elaine O'Neal delivered her second State of the City address emphasizing public safety partnerships, housing initiatives including Bloomberg/Harvard justice-involved housing work, continuation of fare-free transit, and low-carbon concrete sustainability pilots. Council voted unanimously to refer the SCAD (Simplifying Codes for Affordable Development) UDO text amendment back to City-County Planning staff for post-summer scheduling so all seven members could be present. Following public hearings, Council voted 6-0 to adopt a UDO text amendment requiring pet waste receptacles in new developments and along greenways to curb fecal coliform runoff, and amended City Code Sections 70-736 through 70-744 to comply with the state's Neuse Nutrient Strategy. Council also approved the pulled Planning Commission appointment 6-0 after staff verified the nominee's work address lies within city limits.

agenda_items.title: State of the City Address
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal delivered her second State of the City address highlighting collaboration with Durham County, 911 and violence interrupters (Bull City United and The Reformers), affordable housing pressures, Durham's Bloomberg/Harvard leadership initiative for justice-involved individuals' housing, summer youth employment, neighborhood parks, fare-free GoDurham bus service and the GoDurham Access Senior Shuttle, and General Services' low-carbon concrete pilot with Thomas Concrete, CarbonCure, and Skanska.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences and Referral of SCAD UDO Text Amendment Back to Planning Staff
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted unanimously to excuse upcoming May absences before discussing an email from absent member Javiera Caballero and community requests regarding the May 1 SCAD hearing. agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed unanimously across two procedural votes

disagreements.issue: Rezoning of RS-20 and Commercial General Parcel to PDR 13.024 (90-Unit Multifamily Infill near 15-501 and West Cornwallis Road)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on approving a 90-unit predominantly studio and one-bedroom apartment rezoning with five 60%-AMI units and a $100,000 housing fund proffer.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the PDR 13.024 rezoning to allow 90 infill apartments with five 60%-AMI affordable units and $100,000 for the Dedicated Housing Fund.
side_a_arguments: Infill density accommodates urban growth more sustainably than suburban sprawl or the by-right alternative of six single-family homes plus a 5,000-square-foot fast-food drive-thru.
Transportation analysis found negligible intersection delay (LOS B/C at 15-501 and West Cornwallis) and trip generation below the 150 peak-hour trip TIA threshold.

Dissenters questioned traffic level-of-service findings and how school and school-bus impacts were estimated for 90 new residential units.
disagreements.resolution: Rezoning passed 4-3; the accompanying NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement passed 6-1 with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman dissenting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 23, 2023 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Proposed Censure Resolution Against Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman
disagreements.summary: Council members clashed sharply over both the substance and rapid rollout of a draft censure resolution alleging two incidents involving city staff and political campaign work.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance a formal censure resolution for transparency, ethical accountability, and to protect city staff from chilling effects.
side_a_arguments: A second January 2023 incident established a pattern making the earlier incident seven months prior relevant.
Failing to self-police when staff face discipline sends a chilling message to employees.
Members held one-on-one and partnered meetings beforehand, and Jillian Johnson agreed to edit the draft line regarding whether the second staffer was asked or volunteered.
disagreements.side_b_position: Contest the rushed process, late notice, and factual framing of the censure resolution.
side_b_arguments: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman stated she received the draft at 10:30 PM the night before while traveling without sleep and disputed claims she was adequately consulted.

She maintained she never repeated the first incident after meeting with the City Clerk, and that in the second incident an experienced staffer volunteered after HR clearance and took full HR responsibility.
Other members questioned whether Council was independently determining facts or acting on a predetermined report, and Javiera Caballero urged closing unproductive debate.
disagreements.resolution: No vote was taken; Jillian Johnson agreed to circulate an edited version for consideration at a subsequent meeting before Mayor Elaine O'Neal adjourned the session.

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council Meeting March 23, 2023 10 a.m.
meetings.executive_summary: At the March 23, 2023 morning special meeting, the Durham City Council completed its facilitated FY 2023-24 budget request prioritization exercise with Budget Director John Allore and Innovation Team Manager Lindsey Gavin, resolving 11 previously tabled ('yellow') items into 'green' (forwarded to the City Manager) or 'red' categories. Council debated Item #3, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's proposed $200,000 Mentoring Alliance Collaborative Pilot Program, with colleagues questioning whether creating an FTE in the Office on Youth duplicated existing directories and floating a smaller $10,000 matching seed fund with Durham County and DPS. disagreements.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting March 23, 2023 10 a.m.
disagreements.issue: City of Durham Mentoring Alliance Collaborative Pilot Program ($200,000 / FTE vs. Referral List or Matching Seed Fund)
disagreements.summary: Council members differed on whether to advance a $200,000 pilot with a dedicated FTE or pursue a smaller, multi-agency coordination model.
disagreements.side_a_position: Establish a City-funded Mentoring Alliance Collaborative pilot to coordinate youth mentoring partners and combat crisis-level youth violence.
side_a_arguments: Youth gun violence demands proactive prevention and a centralized one-stop shop connecting families to mentoring organizations.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid committing $200,000 or an FTE that alters Office on Youth workflows before identifying specific gaps; use a simpler directory or a small County/DPS matching seed.
side_b_arguments: Ambiguity remains around where the FTE would sit and whether a referral menu/link from the Office on Youth already achieves a one-stop information hub.
A smaller seed allocation (such as $10,000) could test gaps and invite matching funds from Durham County and Durham Public Schools rather than carrying the full $200,000 cost alone.
disagreements.resolution: Time was called at 00:18:59 for workshop categorization, with discussion of scaling down to a smaller matching seed amount before deciding on an FTE.

disagreements.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting March 23, 2023 10 a.m.
disagreements.issue: Hayti Historic Redress Funding Scale and Use of the $30 Million Projected Fund Balance Surplus
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over whether to commit up to $10 million for Hayti historic redress while safeguarding the City's ~$30 million reserve or pursue a larger multi-year/CIP commitment.
disagreements.side_a_position: Put real funding (up to $10 million) on the table for Hayti historic redress without draining the City's rainy-day fund balance.
side_a_arguments: Committing $10 million marks a historic first step that can be supplemented in future budget cycles, CIP updates, and ARPA allocations.
As a self-insured city, Durham cannot raid its entire ~$30 million reserve in one fell swoop without risking fiscal agility.
disagreements.side_b_position: Clarify how the $30 million surplus, ARPA, and CIP align and avoid capping Hayti investment at $10 million without a binding CIP roadmap.
side_b_arguments: If Hayti projects are not placed into the CIP and coordinated with NCDOT, larger transformative investments risk slipping past 2029.
Council should evaluate whether the $30 million surplus can better address department and community priorities alongside ARPA deadlines.
disagreements.resolution: Staff noted green-rated budget priorities totaled $15 million and agreed to return with options balancing ARPA, CIP, fund balance, and general fund sources.

agenda_items.title: Priority Item (Wesley Downs Attachment F) and Consent Agenda

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing on FY 2023-24 Budget and FY 2024-29 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Presided over by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton with a presentation by Budget Director John Allore, the budget public hearing featured speakers (including Kyle Barber, Paul Harvin, Allison Simpson, Anne Lazaridis, and Claire Shellnut) given two minutes each. agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Approval of HOME-ARP Allocation Plan ($4,346,151)

agenda_items.title: FY 2023-24 Annual Action Plan Needs Public Hearing

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 9, 2023 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the March 9, 2023 work session (with Jillian Johnson on excused absence), the Durham City Council reviewed its 22-item draft agenda for the March 20 regular meeting, including a second opioid settlement resolution, ARPA community-rooted public health funding, Merrick Moore Park change order #9 pulled by Mark-Anthony Middleton, the PROWD reintegration grant, and multiple annexation and development items. Javiera Caballero received informal council consensus to bring forward a resolution supporting Temporary Protected Status for Guatemalans. Residents used citizen matters to urge expanded immigrant health and language access and to criticize the 87-page SCAD UDO text amendment (Item 19) ahead of the scheduled March 20 public hearing. Following discussion on scheduling a standalone public hearing date when all seven council members could attend, Council agreed to open the March 20 SCAD public hearing and continue it to a later date, then voted 6-0 to settle the March 20 meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the work session to order at 1:00 PM with six members present and Jillian Johnson on excused absence. Javiera Caballero requested and received thumbs-up consensus from colleagues to bring forward a resolution supporting Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Guatemalans, and Leonardo Williams answered a question raised earlier by DeDreana Freeman.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Reading, Pulled Items, and Public Hearing Clarification
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal read the 22-item draft agenda, covering board appointments, candidate filing fees, a second opioid settlement, ARPA public health funds, Merrick Moore Park CMAR change order #9 (pulled by Mark-Anthony Middleton), the PROWD ex-offender reintegration grant, stormwater/electrical contracts, Lick Creek watershed review (led by DeDreana Freeman), and seven public hearings. When Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman asked to pull Item 19 (SCAD UDO text amendment), the Mayor and City Attorney clarified that public hearing items cannot be pulled at work session and that comments made during citizen matters only enter the official public hearing record once the hearing opens on March 20.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments on Immigrant Equity and SCAD UDO Text Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: One speaker thanked the City for Durham Refugee Day and its shared Immigrant Affairs Coordinator position while urging better multilingual public health and weather-warning outreach. Inter-Neighborhood Council (INC) President Benita Green and subsequent speakers objected to the 85-to-87-page developer-initiated SCAD amendment and argued three-minute citizen comments were inadequate for residents to analyze its technical provisions.

agenda_items.title: Scheduling and Standalone Public Hearing Discussion for SCAD
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members and planning staff discussed moving or dedicating a standalone public hearing night for the SCAD UDO text amendment so residents and both sides could have ample time without seven competing public hearings. After Javiera Caballero clarified she wanted one dedicated public hearing rather than two separate meetings and Mark-Anthony Middleton noted an April 17 travel conflict, Mayor O'Neal emphasized having all seven members present. City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg advised that because March 20 was already advertised, Council should open the public hearing on March 20 and continue it to a staff-coordinated date, which Council endorsed by consensus.

agenda_items.title: Settling the March 20, 2023 City Council Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager recommended placing Items 1 and 3 through 13 on the Consent Agenda and Items 16 through 22 under General Business Agenda Public Hearings. Council approved the settled agenda unanimously among the six members present.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat March 3, 2023 (live stream)
meetings.executive_summary: On March 3, 2023, the Durham City Council held the second day of its FY 2023-24 Budget Retreat at the Department of Water Management facility. City Manager Wanda Page outlined preliminary budget priorities including roughly 5% step and performance pay increases for all employees, additional street maintenance base funding, and up to $25 million in equitable and green infrastructure capital investments, while requesting a two-hour special session to prioritize Council's new budget requests. Council reviewed results from the annual resident survey (673 completed responses highlighting public schools, sidewalks, and transit priorities) and received an update on the City's strategic plan development. Afternoon deliberations focused on draft FY 2023-24 budget guidelines, potential revenue sources, maintaining fare-free transit service, and next steps ahead of budget adoption, with no formal votes taken.

agenda_items.title: Day 2 Opening and City Manager Preliminary Budget Priorities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Management Services staff welcomed Council back to the Water Management facility for Day 2 of the retreat. City Manager Wanda Page highlighted preliminary projections funding ~5% step and performance increases for all city employees, added street maintenance base funding, and up to $25 million for equitable and green infrastructure, and asked Council to schedule a two-hour special session to prioritize council budget requests.

agenda_items.title: Annual Resident Survey Presentation (ETC Institute)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and survey consultant Jason presented findings from 673 completed resident surveys exceeding the 600-response target. Key importance-satisfaction findings pointed to public schools, pedestrian sidewalks, and public transit systems as top resident priorities, alongside demographic breakdowns across Black, Hispanic, and white respondents.

agenda_items.title: Strategic Plan Development Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff reviewed progress on drafting five to seven objectives per strategic goal area, incorporating resident and bilingual survey input alongside department business plans. Goals included delivering city services effectively, advancing the workforce, and building an innovative, high-performing organization.

agenda_items.title: FY 2023-24 Budget Guidelines, Revenue Options, and Fare-Free Transit
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council and budget staff reviewed draft budget guidelines language regarding new revenue sources, property tax capacity, council and staff budget requests, and sustaining fare-free transit service into FY 2023-24. City Manager Wanda Page and Council members closed the retreat by thanking staff for preparing projections amid high vacancy rates and confirming follow-up work sessions ahead of the May budget recommendation and June adoption.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Feb 9, 2023
disagreements.issue: Proposed 10-Cent Plastic Bag Fee Ordinance vs. Education-First Resolution
disagreements.summary: Following a presentation by Don't Waste Durham and university clinic researchers, council members divided over whether to advance an enforceable 10-cent plastic bag fee ordinance with a transition period or begin with a non-binding resolution and public education campaign.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support moving forward with a plastic bag fee ordinance paired with a clear timeline and bilingual public education campaign.
side_a_arguments: Pricing undesirable single-use items is a proven tool to drive both individual and collective behavior change.
An ordinance with an explicit transition timeline (such as 18 months) provides clarity while allowing thorough multilingual outreach.
Other jurisdictions worldwide—including countries with much lower average wealth—have successfully implemented plastic bag restrictions.
disagreements.side_b_position: Support a robust public education campaign and resolution first, viewing a mandatory 10-cent fee ordinance as premature.
side_b_arguments: A 10-cent per-bag fee creates psychological and financial burdens on low-income residents who already pay more for healthy food.
Policing and enforcing local mandates proved challenging during the pandemic.
A robust education campaign coupled with a resolution can build public buy-in before considering an ordinance.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken at the work session; policy discussion left open for further council work.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb. 6, 2023 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 6, 2023 regular meeting (all seven members present), the Durham City Council honored the North Carolina Central University Eagles football team for winning the Celebration Bowl / HBCU National Championship and heard sharp council debate over policing and crisis response—with Jillian Johnson advocating a budget expansion of the HEART team to 24/7 citywide coverage following the Memphis police killing, Mark-Anthony Middleton rejecting comparisons between Durham PD and Memphis PD, and DeDreana Freeman seconding Middleton's call to bring Durham's Police Chief before Council. Later in the night, Council held a contentious deliberation over a ~420-home consolidated annexation and PDR 4.680 rezoning in the Falls/Jordan watershed (One More Carolinas LLC) after residents presented cloudy sink water and cited 'blood red' creek runoff. Over objections from Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman regarding unmitigated sediment runoff and pending county erosion amendments, Council approved the annexation and PDR 4.680 rezoning 4-3 and adopted the consistency statement 6-1.

agenda_items.title: Land Acknowledgment and NCCU Eagles Celebration Bowl Recognition

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jillian Johnson announced a budget request to expand the HEART crisis response team to 24/7 citywide service and referenced a rally with Durham Beyond Policing and the police killing in Memphis. Mark-Anthony Middleton pushed back forcefully against comparing Durham Police to Memphis PD and criticized targeting city staff rather than elected officials, while DeDreana Freeman highlighted the tasing death of Darryl Tyree Williams in Raleigh and seconded Middleton's request to have Durham's Police Chief address Council.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated a 420-home development proposal by One More Carolinas LLC in the Falls/Jordan District B watershed after residents displayed a bottle of turbid sink water and reported blood-red creek runoff near prior developments. Leonardo Williams argued opponents had not linked existing creek impairment to this project, while opposing members urged developers to proffer adherence to Durham County's pending sedimentation and erosion control amendments; Council passed the annexation and PDR 4.680 rezoning 4-3 and the consistency statement 6-1.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency statement passed 6-1

disagreements.issue: HEART Team Expansion Framing and Comparisons Between Durham PD and Memphis PD
disagreements.summary: During council announcements, members clashed over how Durham's HEART alternative crisis response expansion and local policing oversight were framed in light of the police killing in Memphis and the tasing death of Darryl Tyree Williams in Raleigh.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advocate expanding the HEART crisis response program to 24/7 citywide coverage in the upcoming budget and highlight alternative response amid national scrutiny of policing.
side_a_arguments: HEART has demonstrated success and should be funded to operate 24/7 across the entire city.

Community rallies with Durham Beyond Policing underscore public demand for non-police crisis response, heightened by national attention following the police killing in Memphis where Durham's former chief serves.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject equating Durham Police Department with Memphis PD, oppose targeting city employees, and invite the Police Chief before Council to address regional incidents.
side_b_arguments: Durham Police Department is not the Memphis Police Department, and policy disputes should be directed at elected officials on the ballot rather than W-2 city employees.
Bringing Durham's Police Chief before Council allows members to ask direct questions about local practices following regional tragedies such as the tasing death of Darryl Tyree Williams in Raleigh.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; DeDreana Freeman seconded Mark-Anthony Middleton's request to bring the Police Chief before Council during the upcoming budget/oversight cycle.

disagreements.issue: One More Carolinas LLC Annexation and PDR 4.680 Rezoning Amid Creek Sediment Concerns
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on annexing and rezoning land for roughly 420 homes in the Falls/Jordan District B watershed after residents presented turbid sink water and complained of blood-red creek runoff.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and PDR 4.680 rezoning to allow ~420 homes without delaying development over unverified causation claims.
side_a_arguments: The creek has been impaired historically, and opponents have not presented scientific evidence linking this project or recent development activity to increased impairment.
Blanket 'slow down building' arguments do not resolve technical jurisdictional responsibilities, which planning and county staff are working to clarify.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the annexation and rezoning until stronger sedimentation/erosion protections and resident water-quality concerns are addressed.
side_b_arguments: Residents cannot afford private laboratory testing for turbid sink water and blood-red creek runoff and should not have their concerns dismissed as antagonistic.
Council has repeatedly asked developers to proffer compliance with Durham County's stronger sedimentation and erosion control amendments before approval.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and PDR 4.680 rezoning both passed 4-3; the statutory consistency statement subsequently passed 6-1 with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman dissenting.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 19, 2023 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal presided over the January 19, 2023 Durham City Council work session, with Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton on excused absence at the U.S. Conference of Mayors in Washington, D.C. and Leonardo Williams arriving shortly after roll call. During announcements, Jillian Johnson requested consent to bring a draft single-use plastic bag ordinance from Don't Waste Durham to the February 9 work session, and council members recognized youth mentoring programs and the NCCU football team. Council heard public comments from J.J. Henderson Towers residents citing power outages, maintenance failures, and disability accommodation complaints, followed by two major presentations: the Hayti Reborn Justice Movement community violence intervention and mentoring pipeline led by DeDreana Freeman, and an Affordable Housing Deep Dive on the Durham Housing Authority (DHA) led by Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman. Jillian Johnson requested colleague permission to invite Don't Waste Durham to present a draft ordinance limiting single-use plastic bags at the February 9 work session. Other council announcements highlighted Durham youth mentoring finalists honored at the Governor's Mansion, an evening ceremony honoring over 54 mentoring programs, and recognition for the NCCU football team.

agenda_items.title: Draft Agenda Reading

She also noted presentations on the Hayti Reborn Justice Movement (Item 7) and Durham Housing Authority (Item 8), plus five planning public hearings covering consolidated annexations and UDO text/development plan revisions (Items 9-13).

agenda_items.title: J.J. Henderson Towers Resident Concerns and Property Management Complaints
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero managed Citizens' Matters cards as residents raised urgent housing and maintenance complaints. Speakers including Hurley Williams (807 South Duke Street, former J.J. agenda_items.title: Hayti Reborn Justice Movement Presentation

Members discussed mixed-income communities, voucher discrimination by landlords, and the budget trade-off in which raising Fair Market Rents improves unit quality but reduces the number of vouchers DHA can fund. Council members expressed contrasting views on public housing's viability, with some emphasizing mixed-income redevelopment while others defended fully government-funded public housing as a human right.

disagreements.issue: Role of Public Housing vs. Mixed-Income Private-Market Partnerships
disagreements.summary: During the Durham Housing Authority deep-dive discussion, council members diverged on whether concentrated public housing is a failed model that must shift toward mixed-income communities or whether government-funded public housing must be championed as a guaranteed human right.
disagreements.side_a_position: Shift away from concentrated public housing toward structured mixed-income communities that integrate residents socioeconomically rather than isolating low-income households.
side_a_arguments: Concentrated public housing can trap residents in environments with maintenance failures and crime.
Mixed-income communities create better-run, welcoming environments that encourage upward mobility and integration into Durham.
disagreements.side_b_position: Government-funded public housing is 100% the solution and housing must be treated and funded as a guaranteed human right rather than left to a capitalist market.
side_b_arguments: Public housing only struggles when the federal government underfunds it, unlike systems in Western Europe where government investment keeps housing affordable.
Treating housing purely as a market commodity guarantees displacement and homelessness for residents who cannot pay market rates.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion only; no vote taken. (Individual speaker turns in this portion of the digest were not verbally named on the audio except Mayor O'Neal noting prior remarks by Jillian Johnson and Javiera Caballero before the exchange.)

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements, City Manager/Attorney Priority Items, and Excused Absences
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jillian Johnson requested excused absences for March 6 and March 9 due to international travel, and Leonardo Williams announced plans to propose a budget-season task force studying criminal justice and academic disparities facing Black men and boys in Durham. City Manager Wanda Page reported one priority item adding information to the upcoming Homeless Continuum of Care deep-dive presentation, and City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg had no priority items. Council then approved excused absences for Elaine O'Neal, Jillian Johnson, and Mark-Anthony Middleton in three unanimous votes.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Reading
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton read the Consent Agenda into the record, including a resolution supporting ICAN's Cities Appeal for the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (Item 1), ARPA funding for Family Child Care Homes, Reentry Housing Support, and Transitional and Independent Housing (Items 2-4), a Context Systems audiovisual contract amendment (Item 5), a Made in Durham contract (Item 6), and an interlocal agreement amendment for a transit plan governance study (Item 7). Consent action and interim items occur in the truncated middle section of the transcript digest.

agenda_items.title: Kemp Road Residential Consolidated Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement (Bethesda Association LLC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated annexing and extending utilities for the Kemp Road Residential project east of Kemp Road, with opponents citing draft staff growth-management guidance advising against development east of Kemp Road until fire and infrastructure capacity are in place, questioning 600-foot resident mail notifications and an unsuccessful fire station site offer, and warning of a domino effect similar to prior Olive Branch Road rezonings. The applicant committed not to apply for a building permit until a building permit is filed for Fire Station 21, and Fire Department staff noted Station 8 and Station 17 could respond via mutual aid in roughly four to five minutes. Mark-Anthony Middleton defended the project against developer-influence accusations and argued Durham cannot impose a development moratorium, but the annexation motion failed 2-4, leaving Council without jurisdiction to vote on the rezoning or consistency statement.

votes.notes: Elaine O'Neal was absent; Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman was noted as delayed at roll call (00:04:15) and is omitted from confirmed ayes on early procedural votes.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton entertained a motion to excuse Mayor Elaine O'Neal's absence while traveling to the U.S. Conference of Mayors. Leonardo Williams moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded; the clerk reported the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Grant Excused Absences to Council Member Jillian Johnson (March 6 & March 9, 2023)
votes.notes: Elaine O'Neal was absent; Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman was noted as delayed at roll call.
votes.discussion_detail: Following Jillian Johnson's announcement of planned international travel, Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded granting her excused absences for the March 6 regular council meeting and March 9 work session. The clerk reported the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Grant Excused Absence to Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton (Jan. 19, 2023 Work Session)
votes.notes: Elaine O'Neal was absent; Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman was noted as delayed at roll call.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton requested an excused absence for the January 19 work session so he could represent Durham during the second half of the U.S. Conference of Mayors in Washington, D.C. Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded; the clerk reported the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Annexing Kemp Road Residential and Authorizing Utility Extension Agreement with Bethesda Association LLC
votes.notes: Transcript ASR renders 'Kemp Road' as 'Kimb Road'. Elaine O'Neal had an excused absence; the 2 ayes correspond to the remaining seated members present (Mark-Anthony Middleton and Leonardo Williams).
votes.discussion_detail: After extended debate over draft growth boundaries east of Kemp Road, fire service coverage, and resident notifications, Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded the annexation and utility extension agreement with Bethesda Association LLC. The clerk closed the vote and reported the motion failed 4-2 (2 ayes, 4 nays), with DeDreana Freeman, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, Jillian Johnson, and Javiera Caballero voting no. City Attorney advice confirmed no jurisdiction remained for the rezoning or consistency statement motions.

disagreements.issue: Kemp Road Residential Annexation East of Draft Infrastructure Growth Boundary
disagreements.summary: Council split 2-4 over whether to approve a consolidated annexation and utility extension agreement east of Kemp Road ahead of finalized Comprehensive Plan/infrastructure rules and Fire Station 21 construction.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and utility extension agreement based on its project merits and fire-permit condition rather than uncodified draft policy lines.
side_a_arguments: The draft growth-boundary guidance is not yet codified law and Council should not cede decision-making to draft staff proposals.
Durham cannot legally enact a development moratorium and is one of the fastest-growing cities in the country.
The developer proffered not to seek building permits until Fire Station 21 permits are applied for, and Stations 8 and 17 are within 4-5 minutes via mutual aid.
Opposing growth under slogans like 'preserve rural Durham' can function as coded resistance to urbanization, and supporters should not be accused of being in developers' pockets.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject annexation east of Kemp Road until municipal infrastructure, fire coverage, and adopted growth policies are in place.
side_b_arguments: Planning staff are neutral arbiters whose guidance advises against building east of Kemp Road until infrastructure capacity improves.
Approving one project across the line creates a domino effect into unready areas, repeating past 4-3 Olive Branch Road rezoning controversies.
Concerns remained over 600-foot resident notification delivery and an earlier proposed fire station site across a stream that proved unviable.
disagreements.resolution: Motion to annex and authorize the Utility Extension Agreement failed 2-4 at 03:19:37, rendering the companion rezoning and consistency motions without jurisdiction.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 5, 2023 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal presided over the January 5, 2023 Durham City Council work session, with Javiera Caballero on excused absence and DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams arriving after roll call. Council unanimously approved City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg's priority item to hold a closed session at the end of the meeting regarding Fourth Circuit litigation (Plaintiff Parent v. City of Durham). After hearing public comments on a dedicated Duke-to-UNC bicycle path, Wellons Village gun violence and ShotSpotter funding, and fire/EMS coverage for new developments, Council heard two deep-dive briefings: the Durham Homeless Continuum of Care (led by Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman) and the DCHC MPO FY 2021-22 Annual Report (led by Mark-Anthony Middleton). Council then voted unanimously to settle the January 17 regular meeting agenda before adjourning into closed session at 3:08 PM.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and City Attorney Closed Session Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal opened the work session, noting Javiera Caballero's excused absence and delayed arrivals for DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams. City Manager Wanda Page and the City Clerk had no priority items, while City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg requested a closed session at the conclusion of business under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation on Plaintiff Parent v. City of Durham, Michelle Susie Scott, Pinnacle in the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals. Council unanimously approved accepting the priority item and holding the closed session.

agenda_items.title: Draft Agenda Reading and Pulled Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal read the draft agenda covering an ICAN nuclear weapons treaty resolution (Item 1), ARPA grants for family child care, reentry housing, and transitional housing (Items 2-4), a broadcasting support contract amendment (Item 5), a Made in Durham contract (Item 6, pulled by DeDreana Freeman), a transit governance study ILA amendment (Item 7), presentations (Items 8-9), and four planning public hearings (Items 10-13). A council member thanked staff, the Biden administration, and Congressional Democrats for moving ARPA funding rapidly to the community.

agenda_items.title: Citizens' Matters: Duke-UNC Bike Path, Wellons Village Safety, and Development Infrastructure
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Phil Reamer urged Durham to prioritize long-haul 8-to-10-mile separated bikeways—specifically a dedicated bicycle path between Duke University and UNC-Chapel Hill—rather than short painted lanes along high-speed roads. John Tate Dunston addressed New Year's Day shootings in Wellons Village, arguing ShotSpotter funds should instead pay for four additional police officers to patrol neighborhoods. Another speaker (preceding a truncated middle section) raised concerns about developments lacking existing fire/EMS coverage and urged stronger developer proffers ahead of January 17 hearings.

agenda_items.title: Affordable Housing Deep Dive: Durham Homeless Continuum of Care
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Led by Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, Continuum of Care staff (including Mr. Davis) reviewed federal HUD homelessness prioritization tiers and explained that federal rules require rental assistance payments go to third-party landlords and utilities rather than direct stipends favored by DeDreana Freeman. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton praised Durham's ~$2 million dedicated housing penny investment and announced plans to propose extending and expanding Durham's guaranteed income pilot during the upcoming budget cycle. Mayor Elaine O'Neal requested the CoC's top three legislative and budget needs for the next 12 months.

agenda_items.title: DCHC MPO FY 2021-22 Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Led by Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, DCHC MPO Executive Director Doug Placzynski presented the MPO's annual report, highlighting Vision Zero safety work, upgraded public involvement policies, and repositioning the MPO to Triangle J Council of Governments (TJCOG). Placzynski projected a 10-15% increase in local match dues—roughly $30,000-$40,000 more for Durham above its current ~$1-per-resident contribution toward the $5.5 million MPO budget—to free City Transportation staff to focus on delivering local projects.

agenda_items.title: Settling the January 17 Agenda and Adjourning to Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page recommended placing Items 1-7 on the Consent Agenda and Items 10-13 on General Business Public Hearings. Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded settling the agenda, which passed unanimously by show of left hands before Council adjourned into closed session at 3:08 PM.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Jan. 3, 2023 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal presided over the first Durham City Council meeting of 2023 on January 3, with six members present and Javiera Caballero on an excused absence. Ceremonial recognitions included proclaiming January 2023 as Courage Month and reading two National Mentoring Month proclamations, alongside remarks by DeDreana Freeman urging community-level intervention to protect youth before law enforcement involvement. Council unanimously passed the Consent Agenda (Items 1-7) by a 6-0 show of hands, heard the staff presentation on Welcome Venture Park (Item 9, with Mark-Anthony Middleton disclosing a non-financial notification-area relationship), and unanimously approved (6-0) the Aura Hillandale West rezoning to Planned Development Residential 59.102 after neighborhood discussion of tree preservation and sidewalk alignment. Council also unanimously approved (6-0) the Chapel Hill Road convenience store rezoning to Commercial Neighborhood before adjourning at 8:23 PM.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Courage Month, and National Mentoring Month Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal opened the meeting with silent meditation, DeDreana Freeman led the Pledge of Allegiance, and roll call recorded six members present with Javiera Caballero excused. O'Neal proclaimed January 2023 as Courage Month, and council presented two National Mentoring Month proclamations recognizing local youth programs including D.F. Forbes Youth Foundation, Durham Proud, 100 Black Men of Triangle East, Bull City Bulldogs, We Are Kings, and We Are Queens. Freeman urged residents to engage directly with neighborhood youth to prevent violence before police or news cameras arrive.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Updates and Consent Agenda Approval (Items 1-7)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page reported revised development plans and proffers for Item 9 (Welcome Venture Park) and Item 10 (Aura Hillandale West), while the City Attorney and City Clerk had no priority items. Mayor O'Neal read Consent Agenda Items 1-7, including board appointments, the November 2022 bid report, permit fee reimbursement for disabled veteran housing construction, ARPA Multifamily Acquisition Support, a wireless lease at 1318 East Pettigrew Street, and a John R. McAdams contract. Council approved the Consent Agenda unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Welcome Venture Park Zoning Map Change
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton opened the Item 9 public hearing and disclosed for transparency that an organization where he serves as a principal is a major landowner within the notification area without any financial conflict. Planner Brooke Roper reported the Planning Commission recommended approval 11-0 for Industrial Light with a development plan consistent with the Future Land Use Map, requiring three motions. The applicant's presentation and vote occur within the truncated middle section of the transcript.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Approval: Aura Hillandale West Zoning Map Change (PDR 59.102)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the Aura Hillandale West request to rezone property from Industrial Light to Planned Development Residential 59.102 alongside a Future Land Use Map change to High Density Residential and Recreation & Open Space, noting an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation on October 11, 2022. Seven proponents signed up and nearby residents including Julie Mancuso Craig and Karen Cantor addressed the project, with speakers urging preservation of existing trees by combining city and developer sidewalks. Staff noted forestry staff work to minimize root impacts and the applicant noted neighborhood-agreed replacement plantings, after which Council unanimously approved all three required motions.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Approval: Chapel Hill Road Convenience Store Zoning Map Change
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Led by Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton, planner Brooke Roper presented Christopher Kowski's request for 0.2 acres at 2945 Chapel Hill Road and 3036 University Drive to rezone from RS-8 and RS-10 to Commercial Neighborhood with a text-only development plan to reconstruct the existing convenience store. No members of the public spoke on the item, and Council unanimously passed both the zoning ordinance and consistency statement motions.

agenda_items.title: Hayti Reborn Work Session Scheduling and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman confirmed scheduling the Hayti Reborn Justice Movement presentation for the January 19 work session and clarified it did not concern Fayette Place. Mayor O'Neal closed with remarks honoring Courage Month, victims of shootings, and longtime resident Anita Green's admonition to 'be a kind human being' before adjourning at 8:23 PM.
