meetings.title: Durham City Council Sept.19, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Held on Monday, September 19, 2022 (indexed under 2022-09-20) with all seven Council members present and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presiding over public hearings while Mayor Elaine O'Neal rested her voice, Council approved pay adjustments for its three direct-report officers (7-0), the Consent Agenda (7-0), and pulled Item 14 renewing Bull City United (7-0). On Item 27, Council approved the one-year $197,500 ShotSpotter gunshot-detection pilot 5-2 over dissents from Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson. In land-use public hearings, Council approved 1409 Doc Nichols Road (60 townhomes, 3 Habitat homes) 5-2 (O'Neal and Freeman opposed; consistency 7-0), narrowly passed 7926 Massey Chapel Road (28 townhomes, 1 Habitat unit) 4-3 (O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman opposed; consistency 5-2 after clicker corrections), approved five street closings 6-1 by hand vote (Freeman opposed), and unanimously backed the 182-unit Dearborn Drive affordable/VFW project and 44-unit Wabash Parcels townhomes 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations (Melissa Wade Day, Algonquin Tennis Club, Diaper Need, Dementia, Grace Month) & Charter Officer Raises
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council honored gospel broadcaster Melissa Wade, celebrated the centennial of the historic Algonquin Tennis Club with Dr. Eugene Victor Maffo, proclaimed Diaper Need Awareness Week and World Alzheimer's/Dementia Awareness Day, and read the Grace Month proclamation in honor of Chief Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson. Mark-Anthony Middleton also publicly reported and Council voted 7-0 to approve annual performance salary adjustments for City Manager Wanda Page ($255,000 to $265,200), City Attorney Kim Rehberg ($206,700 to $219,102), and City Clerk Diana Schreiber ($103,175 to $107,302).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval & Pulled Item 14 (Bull City United Contract Renewal)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the Consent Agenda (excluding pulled Item 14 and Item 27 on GBA) 7-0, including the $4.03M Water Management facility change order, Gang Reduction Strategy, Legal Aid DEAR renewal, and NICE intelligence center contract. Resident Dante Dunstan spoke strongly in favor of Item 14 (Bull City United), urging Council not to let one individual's misstep jeopardize funding for credible violence interrupters, and Council renewed Bull City United 7-0.

agenda_items.title: ShotSpotter Response Services Agreement ($197,500 One-Year Pilot)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Before the vote on the one-year ShotSpotter gunshot-detection contract, Javiera Caballero argued against investing $197,500 in technology she viewed as unproven elsewhere and likely to heighten police presence in Black and brown neighborhoods rather than funding root-cause prevention, while Jillian Johnson opposed the contract for similar civil-liberties and efficacy concerns. Mark-Anthony Middleton countered that Council should judge the vetted pilot based on Durham's own Wilson Center evaluation data rather than outside composites, and the contract passed 5-2.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: 1409 Doc Nichols Road (60 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Andy Lester and Jared Edens of Edens Land Corp presented a 60-townhome proposal (PDR 7.245) including a revised commitment to donate three completed townhouses (rather than building pads) to Habitat for Humanity, 100-year stormwater detention, double silt fencing, and DPS/housing donations, after a 5-5 Planning Commission tie. Neighbors and advocates clashed over blasting damage, well-water sediment, Highway 98/Doc Nichols traffic, and rural sprawl versus housing supply and 3 Habitat units, with Council passing annexation and rezoning 5-2 (O'Neal and Freeman opposed) and the consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: 7926 Massey Chapel Road (28 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Edens Land Corp proposed annexing 5.828 acres at 7926 Massey Chapel Road and rezoning from RR to PDR 4.928 for 28 townhouses, committing one completed Habitat for Humanity townhome, a Massey Chapel sidewalk to the American Tobacco Trail (subject to NCDOT approval), 100-year sediment ponds, and weekend construction limits following a 7-7 Planning Commission tie. Neighbors Pat Brocchino and Jeremy Tarr objected to three-story height, uphill lighting, traffic near Southpoint Mall, and speculative marketing; Council passed annexation and rezoning 4-3 (O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman opposed) and the consistency statement 5-2 after correcting clicker errors.

agenda_items.title: Permanent Street Closings: Greenmount Dr, Arborstone Way, Broadstone Ct, Flatstone Ct, Upland Meadows Ln
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Cole Renigar presented Steve Puckett's request (SC2200004) to permanently close five platted rights-of-way running parallel to East Ramseur Street and the North Carolina Railroad to recombine parcels into 18.78-acre and 13.63-acre lots for future development east of Chandler Road. With no public speakers and electronic clickers replaced by raised-hand voting for the remainder of the night, Council approved the street closings 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Dearborn Drive Multi-Family (182 Affordable Units & VFW/BCA Civic Space)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton disclosed his nonprofit owns nearby Braggtown land with no financial inducement, Andy Lester and attorney Nil Ghosh presented LDG Development's RU-5 to PDR 19.401 rezoning (Planning Commission 11-0) for 182 apartments averaging 60% AMI or below for 30 years plus 5,000 sq ft of deeded civic space for VFW Post operations and Braggtown Community Association offices. VFW Commander Larry Coleman, Vanessa Mason Evans, and Donna Frederick strongly praised the partnership and urged future city support to add 30% AMI units; Council praised the project unanimously and approved both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Wabash Parcels (44 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Dr. William Chambers, attorney Floyd McKissick III, engineer Landon Lovelace, and former State Senator/Council Member Floyd McKissick Jr. presented a 9.96-acre infill rezoning at 1500/1521 Wabash Street and 1214 Truman Street from RU-5 to PDR 5.170 for 44 owner-occupied townhomes targeted near $300,000 for NCCU/Durham Tech workers, with 32% tree save, Greenway easement along Third Fork Creek, and $25,000 housing fund proffer (Planning Commission 8-5). Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0 before adjourning at 11:08 PM.

votes.item_title: Approve Annual Salary Adjustments for City Manager, City Attorney, and City Clerk
votes.notes: Mover and seconder voices ('so move... second') were not named aloud by the chair.
votes.discussion_detail: Following Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton's closed-session evaluation report, Council voted 7-0 by electronic vote to approve fiscal year salary increases for City Manager Wanda Page ($255,000 to $265,200), City Attorney Kim Rehberg ($206,700 to $219,102), and City Clerk Diana Schreiber ($103,175 to $107,302).

votes.item_title: Approve Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 14 and GBA Item 27)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded approving the Consent Agenda excluding resident-pulled Item 14 and General Business Agenda Item 27, passing 7-0 by electronic vote.

votes.item_title: Item 14 (Pulled): Approve Bull City United Update and Contract Renewal
votes.discussion_detail: Following testimony from Dante Dunstan supporting Bull City United's community violence interruption efforts, DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded renewing the Bull City United contract, passing 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Approve ShotSpotter Response Services Agreement ($197,500 One-Year Pilot)
votes.discussion_detail: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman moved and Leonardo Williams seconded approving the one-year ShotSpotter gunshot-detection contract. After Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson stated their opposition and Mark-Anthony Middleton defended evaluating the local pilot, the electronic vote passed 5-2.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and UEA for 1409 Doc Nichols Road
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded annexing 1409 Doc Nichols Road and authorizing a utility extension agreement with Edens Land Corp, passing 5-2 with Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for 1409 Doc Nichols Road (RR to PDR 7.245)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded rezoning 1409 Doc Nichols Road from Rural Residential (RR) to Planned Development Residential 7.245 (PDR 7.245) for up to 60 townhouses including three completed Habitat units, passing 5-2 with O'Neal and Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 1409 Doc Nichols Road
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for 1409 Doc Nichols Road; after correcting an initial 6-1 clicker display involving Mayor O'Neal, the Clerk reported 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and UEA for 7926 Massey Chapel Road
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded annexing 7926 Massey Chapel Road effective September 30, 2022 and entering a UEA with Edens Land Corp. After Mayor O'Neal corrected her malfunctioning clicker from 'not voting' to 'no', the vote was recorded 4-3 with O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for 7926 Massey Chapel Road (RR to PDR 4.928)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded rezoning 7926 Massey Chapel Road from RR to PDR 4.928 for up to 28 townhouses with one completed Habitat unit, passing 4-3 with O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 7926 Massey Chapel Road
votes.notes: After this item, Mayor O'Neal requested hand votes for the remainder of the meeting due to persistent electronic clicker failures.
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the consistency statement for 7926 Massey Chapel Road. After clicker malfunctions initially displayed an invalid abstention for DeDreana Freeman (who confirmed voting no) and a false no for Mayor O'Neal (who confirmed pressing yes), the final count was recorded 5-2.

votes.item_title: Item 35: Adopt Order Permanently Closing Greenmount Dr, Arborstone Way, Broadstone Ct, Flatstone Ct, and Upland Meadows Ln
votes.notes: Mover's name was cut/inaudible in ASR ('councilman ...').
votes.discussion_detail: Switched to raised-hand voting after clicker failures and seconded by Javiera Caballero, Council approved closing five platted rights-of-way east of Chandler Road by a 6-1 vote with DeDreana Freeman dissenting.

votes.item_title: Item 36 (Motion 1): Adopt Zoning Map Change for Dearborn Drive Multi-Family (RU-5 to PDR 19.401)
votes.discussion_detail: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman moved and Leonardo Williams seconded rezoning three Braggtown parcels from RU-5 to PDR 19.401 for 182 affordable apartments (60% AMI average, 30 years) and 5,000 sq ft of VFW/BCA civic space, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 36 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Dearborn Drive Multi-Family
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for the Dearborn Drive project, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 37 (Motion 1): Adopt Zoning Map Change for Wabash Parcels (RU-5 to PDR 5.170)
votes.discussion_detail: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman moved and Jillian Johnson seconded rezoning 1500/1521 Wabash Street and 1214 Truman Street from RU-5 to PDR 5.170 for up to 44 townhomes with a $25,000 housing fund donation and Greenway easement, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 37 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Wabash Parcels
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded (with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman also seconding) adopting the statutory consistency statement for Wabash Parcels, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

disagreements.issue: ShotSpotter Gunshot-Detection One-Year Pilot Approval
disagreements.summary: Council voted 5-2 to launch the $197,500 one-year ShotSpotter acoustic gunshot-detection pilot after sharp disagreement over effectiveness, civil liberties, and police deployment in Black and brown neighborhoods.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the vetted one-year pilot to test whether acoustic gunfire detection speeds emergency medical response and evidence collection.
side_a_arguments: Independent evaluation by Duke's Wilson Center will measure real Durham data before any permanent renewal.
Faster alerts can locate shooting victims even when no 911 call is made.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose ShotSpotter and invest instead in proven root-cause violence prevention.
side_b_arguments: Other cities found high false-positive rates, minimal violence reduction, and heightened unnecessary police encounters in Black and brown neighborhoods.
$197,500 would yield greater safety returns in youth programs, mental health, and violence interruption.
disagreements.resolution: The ShotSpotter contract passed 5-2.

disagreements.issue: 1409 Doc Nichols Road Rural Annexation, Blasting/Well Water Impacts, and Housing Supply
disagreements.summary: Following a 5-5 Planning Commission tie, Council passed 1409 Doc Nichols Road 5-2 while splitting over neighbor reports of well turbidity, blasting, and Highway 98 traffic versus housing supply and three completed Habitat townhomes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 60-townhome development given upgraded Habitat, stormwater, and erosion proffers and urgent regional housing demand.
side_a_arguments: Denying the rezoning leaves worse outcomes—either luxury single-family homes on well/septic or warehouses—while restricting supply drives downtown rents upward.
The developer added three completed Habitat townhomes, double silt fencing, and 100-year stormwater ponds.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexing County parcels lacking city water/sewer protections and infrastructure capacity for surrounding rural residents.
side_b_arguments: Existing County residents face well-water sediment and blasting fears without automatic city utility extensions or pre-blast inspections.
Cumulative eastern annexations outpace roads, schools, and emergency response planning.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 5-2; consistency passed 7-0.

disagreements.issue: 7926 Massey Chapel Road Townhomes Compatibility and Traffic Near Southpoint
disagreements.summary: Following a 7-7 Planning Commission tie, Council split 4-3 on approving 28 townhomes squeezed between rural homes and Southpoint retail.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve 28 transitional townhomes with one Habitat unit, sidewalk to the American Tobacco Trail, and 100-year stormwater controls rather than four million-dollar by-right houses.
side_a_arguments: Reducing density from 40 to 28 units and extending public water/sewer to neighbors with failing septic provides meaningful mitigation.
Townhomes near retail and the American Tobacco Trail are far more attainable than $1M single-family estates.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject the rezoning due to neighborhood traffic congestion, flood-zone/stormwater concerns, height transition, and unverified sidewalk feasibility.
side_b_arguments: Southpoint weekend traffic already congests Massey Chapel Road, and no traffic study was required below 150 peak trips.
Neighbors disputed site elevation/light-pole spillover and questioned NCDOT approval for sidewalks.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency passed 5-2 after correcting clicker errors.

meetings.title: City Council Retreat- September 9, 2022 [Livestream]
meetings.executive_summary: At this five-hour facilitated City Council Housing Retreat held at Durham's new Water Management/Public Works facility with all seven Council members present, facilitators guided Council through a 'Wall of Wonder' retrospective spanning the 1980s through 2022 and future visions toward 2040. Members reflected on Durham's historical housing milestones—urban renewal, Hayti, the $95M housing bond, dedicated penny taxes, Eviction Diversion, Expanding Housing Choices, and the 2020-2021 pandemic—while surfacing sharp philosophical disagreements over market-rate supply versus public-interest housing subsidies, public housing stereotypes, growth's environmental impacts, and institutional trust. No formal votes were taken during the workshop; Council closed by calling for concrete data-driven follow-ups from DataWorks NC, community equity benchmarks, and clearer affordability definitions.

agenda_items.title: Retreat Opening, Personal Housing Stories & 1980s-2022 'Wall of Wonder' Timeline
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Facilitators opened the retreat at the new Public Works/Water Management/Fleet complex with each Council member sharing an image or personal story about home and stability—ranging from Mayor Elaine O'Neal's childhood home built on Morehead Avenue by her factory-worker father to Leonardo Williams's post-eviction search and DeDreana Freeman's loss of her sister. City staff and Council then mapped Durham's housing trajectory from the 1980s through 2022, highlighting Hayti/Southside redevelopment, the penny tax and $95M affordable housing bond, Expanding Housing Choices, Eviction Diversion, and pandemic dislocation.

agenda_items.title: Debate Over Market Supply, Affordable Housing Priorities, Environmental Stewardship & 2040 Vision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reviewing the Wall of Wonder and envisioning 2040, Council engaged in candid, occasionally tense exchanges over market-rate development versus targeted low-income subsidies, gentrification, public-housing stereotypes, water/tree stewardship, and how Council votes are framed publicly. Leonardo Williams urged building for high-income arrivals to shield historic neighborhoods while arguing public housing was meant to be transitional; Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman defended housing as a human right and pushed back against stereotyping low-wage, senior, and disabled residents; and Mark-Anthony Middleton pressed for concrete tax/bond policy tools and civility. Mayor O'Neal closed by outlining upcoming educational sessions including DataWorks NC.

disagreements.issue: Market-Rate Housing Supply, Public Housing Responsibility, and Environmental Trade-Offs
disagreements.summary: During the five-hour housing retreat, Council divided sharply on whether building market-rate housing prevents displacement, how public housing and low-wage workers are framed, and whether pro-growth annexations compromise water and environmental stewardship.
disagreements.side_a_position: Build supply across all price tiers to absorb high-wealth newcomers, rely on concrete bonds/taxes for subsidies, and view public housing as transitional.
side_a_arguments: Leonardo Williams argued Durham must create higher-end supply so $189,000+ earners do not bid away downtown Black neighborhoods, adding that public housing was meant to be transitional and some people walk off $19/hour jobs.

Mark-Anthony Middleton contended government action only materializes through budgets, bonds ($95M), and dedicated taxes, and pushed back against framing pro-growth votes as 'harm' or 'poisoning water'.
disagreements.side_b_position: Treat housing as a human right, prioritize deep subsidies for low-wage, senior, and disabled residents, and center environmental stewardship in growth decisions.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman pushed back against stigmatizing public housing residents, noting many are elderly, disabled on fixed Social Security, or working multiple low-wage jobs.
DeDreana Freeman and Mayor Elaine O'Neal emphasized protecting tree canopy, water quality, and longtime residents rather than letting private developers dictate Durham's growth pattern.
disagreements.resolution: No formal votes were taken; Council agreed to continue housing deep-dive sessions including a data presentation from DataWorks NC.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 8, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the September 8, 2022 work session with all seven members present, Council expressed condolences to DeDreana Freeman on her sister's passing, suspended rules to approve a $13.52M FAA Airport Improvement Grant for RDU (7-0 across priority/suspension/grant motions), and heard Emancipate NC and Darryl Howard demand police-accountability reparations during Citizen Matters. Council scrutinized pulled items including the Master Aging Plan (Item 9), Gang Reduction Strategy (Item 15), a $4.03M Water Management facility change order (Item 21), the $197,500 ShotSpotter pilot (Item 27, moved to GBA by Caballero), and NICE intelligence software (Item 30). Council also heard Bull City United's annual report showing violence reductions across six census tracts, Tim Flora's FY22 Q4 financial update ($7.4M general fund surplus, DPAC recovery, parking deficit), and Craig Davis Properties' $5M offer for the Durham Center Parking Deck—which drew strong skepticism over lost public parking and off-site affordable housing—before settling the September 19 agenda (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Announcements, Priority Items, FAA $13.52M RDU Grant Suspension & Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Opening with condolences to DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson requested an unbiased environmental/flocculant analysis of the Eno/Falls/Searles Basin following the September 6 Leesville hearing, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman celebrated HEART's first 199 non-police calls. Council approved the City Manager's priority items (7-0), suspended rules (7-0) to approve RDU's $13,522,729 FAA Airport Improvement Grant and authorize City Manager Wanda Page to sign (7-0 each), and accepted the Clerk's priority item referring Item 4 (Planning Commission appointment) back to the Clerk (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Walltown Northgate Mall Equitable Redevelopment & Emancipate NC Police Accountability Requests
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Brandon Williams of the Walltown Community Association urged Council to convene a collaborative planning table with Northwood Investors and Duke on Northgate Mall redevelopment and invest part of Durham's remaining $22.5M ARPA funds in affordable housing, transit, and green space. Following a legal caution from City Attorney Kim Rehberg on active litigation, Emancipate NC Executive Director Dawn Blagrove, Darryl Howard (wrongfully imprisoned 22 years), and organizer Adid Wacuri urged Council to accept responsibility and pay reparations for historic police misconduct.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: Master Aging Plan, Gang Strategy, DWM Change Order, ShotSpotter & NICE Center
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned prior-year unspent funds on Item 9 (Master Aging Plan) and single-bid supply-chain and EV-conduit costs in Item 21's $4,028,998 Gilbane Water Management facility change order, as well as the one-year structure of Item 30's NICE intelligence center contract. On Item 15 (Gang Reduction Strategy), Leonardo Williams pressed manager Jim Stuit for proactive youth metrics while DeDreana Freeman and Dr. Holsey-Hyman defended holistic system-wide supports. On Item 27 (ShotSpotter), Police Chief Patrice Andrews and Jason Sheese outlined Priority-2 response rules and Duke's Wilson Center external evaluation; Jillian Johnson and Middleton sparred over evaluation standards, and Javiera Caballero moved ShotSpotter to GBA.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Items 9, 15, 21, 30 on Consent; Item 27 on GBA

agenda_items.title: Bull City United Fourth-Quarter and Annual Violence Interruption Update

Council members praised the neighborhood-based credibility and life-saving mediation work.

agenda_items.title: FY 2021-2022 Fourth-Quarter Unaudited Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director Tim Flora reported a $7.4M unaudited general fund net surplus through June 30, 2022 (revenues $20.3M over budget fueled by online sales taxes, expenditures $12.9M under budget due to salary vacancies), $11.4M water/sewer surplus, $5.5M transit surplus alongside bus-delivery delays, a $693,700 parking fund loss addressed via July rate increases, and DPAC's record $1.4M net increase across 454,000 guests. Following a brief moment of silence for Queen Elizabeth II's passing, Council questioned Flora on tax-base indicators, bus deliveries, and parking fee communication.

agenda_items.title: Craig Davis Properties Durham Center Parking Deck Proposal, Appointments & Agenda Settling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Craig Davis Properties presented a $5M offer (based on $4.9M reconciled appraisals plus a Morris Street sliver) to purchase the city's Durham Center Parking Deck, demolish the west half to build a 32-story, 308-unit market-rate tower ('The James'), provide $650,000 to the affordable housing fund (~6 off-site units), and leave 82-84 daytime P1 public spaces plus ~300 after-hours east spaces. Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar explained the 1980s three-party air-rights agreement; Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, Javiera Caballero, and Mayor O'Neal objected to losing 719 city-owned spaces near Carolina Theatre and demanded on-site affordable units, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and Leonardo Williams urged weighing tax revenue, $5M leverage, and downtown housing supply. disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 8, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Craig Davis Properties $5M Offer for Durham Center Parking Deck: On-Site Affordable Units and Public Parking Loss
disagreements.summary: Council members diverged sharply in response to Craig Davis Properties' presentation to purchase the Durham Center Parking Deck for $5M and build a 32-story market-rate tower with a $650K off-site housing contribution.
disagreements.side_a_position: Demand on-site affordable housing units and preserve downtown public parking near Carolina Theatre rather than accepting a $650K fund payment.
side_a_arguments: Because the city owns the deck and holds leverage over air-rights changes, Council should require affordable units inside the building itself rather than allowing exclusively luxury $7,000/month three-bedroom apartments downtown.

Reducing 719 city-owned parking spaces directly across from Carolina Theatre and the Convention Center to ~82-84 daytime P1 spaces and 300 evening/weekend spaces weakens city assets and accessibility.
disagreements.side_b_position: Evaluate whether $5M in proceeds, nearly $926K in annual tax revenue, and 308 market-rate units outweigh holding an underperforming parking deck.
side_b_arguments: Adding downtown residential supply absorbs high-income newcomers who otherwise bid up older neighborhood homes and trigger tax-driven displacement.
Middleton argued Council must ask whether the deck currently generates $5M in value and examine residents' quality of life when affordable units sit in high-cost entertainment districts.
disagreements.resolution: Informational presentation only; staff and the developer took Council's feedback back for further negotiation before any formal agenda item.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 8, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: ShotSpotter Evaluation Standards and Risk of False-Positive Policing Harm
disagreements.summary: During discussion of pulled Item 27, members clashed over how ShotSpotter's one-year pilot should be evaluated and weighed against potential harms.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support testing ShotSpotter with Duke's Wilson Center external evaluation and judge it on local Durham data, noting even one saved life matters.
side_a_arguments: Durham should not rely on worst-case policing examples from other cities and already evaluates ShotSpotter more rigorously than pilots like Participatory Budgeting.
NCCU Chancellor Akinleye expressed support for technology near campus, and faster Priority-2 alerts can get aid to victims faster.
disagreements.side_b_position: Weigh potential harms—false gunfire alerts, wrongful arrests, and aggressive police responses—equally alongside any potential benefits and scrutinize PB comparisons.
side_b_arguments: Participatory Budgeting is evaluated every cycle and does not carry life-or-liberty policing risks.
If ShotSpotter harms or causes the false imprisonment of one resident, that cost must weigh just as heavily as saving a life.
disagreements.resolution: Javiera Caballero pulled Item 27 from Consent to the September 19 General Business Agenda for a separate vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Sept. 6, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present on Tuesday, September 6, 2022 (following Labor Day), Council opened with proclamations for Durham's first-ever Welcoming Week and National Recovery Month, handled priority referrals (Fontanelle and Gilbert Street closings and Item 4 Planning Commission appointment), approved the Consent Agenda 7-0 by raised hand after clicker troubles, and adopted Item 9 honoring Dr. Doc J. Jordan and Carrie Thomas Jordan Highway (7-0). The session centered on a marathon public hearing for Item 19 (5909 & 6301 Leesville Road, 330 townhomes across 88 acres, Planning Commission 9-1 denial), where residents presented sediment vials and well filters while staff and county erosion chief Ryan Eves clarified flocculants and stormwater rules. After the applicant added proffers ($45K to DPS, 50% mass-grading cap, right-of-way dedication, 30-foot street yard), annexation and rezoning passed 4-3 (consistency 7-0). Council closed by unanimously approving Item 20 (90-unit East Geer Street multi-family affordable project, 7-0) after debating 9% LIHTC competition with DHA.

agenda_items.title: Welcoming Week, Recovery Month, Priority Referrals & Consent Agenda (Items 1-3, 5-8, 10-18, 24)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal proclaimed Welcoming Week and Mark-Anthony Middleton presented National Recovery Month; council members also expressed solidarity with Jackson, Mississippi and Enfield, North Carolina and congratulated NCCU and Duke football wins. City Manager Wanda Page referred Items 21 (Fontanelle Street) and 22 (Gilbert Street) back to Planning and updated attachments for Items 19 and 20, while Deputy Clerk Ashley Wyatt referred Item 4 (Planning Commission appointment) back—prompting Middleton to request an inquiry into whether Council had already voted. Council approved the Consent Agenda (excluding Items 4, 9, 21, 22) 7-0 by hand vote.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Designating Fayetteville Street Portion as Dr. Doc J. Jordan and Carrie Thomas Jordan Highway
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Moved up in the agenda by Mark-Anthony Middleton as a celebratory item, family members Delores Hollinger and DeLantae Hollinger spoke on the civic, education, and historic legacy of Dr. Doc J. Jordan and Carrie Thomas Jordan along Fayetteville Street. Council unanimously adopted the commemorative highway designation resolution 7-0 by raised hand.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: 5909 & 6301 Leesville Road (330 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff and engineer Tim Sivers (Horvath Associates) presented an 88-acre annexation and RR-to-PDR 3.75 rezoning for 330 townhomes with 3% affordable units (~10 units) and 50% open space after a 9-1 Planning Commission denial. Opponents brought 'tomato soup' creek vials and clogged well filters citing Grove Park runoff, mass grading, blasting, flocculants, and school capacity, while county erosion manager Ryan Eves and Planning Director Sara Young explained polyacrylamides and modern stormwater detention. Sivers added proffers raising DPS funding to $45,000, capping simultaneous mass grading at 50%, dedicating 25-ft right-of-way, and adding a 30-ft street yard; annexation and rezoning passed 4-3 and consistency passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: East Geer Street Residential (90 Affordable/Workforce Units)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Brooke Roper presented East Geer Street Ventures LLC's (corrected in motion to Southern Repair Service LLC) request for a 90-unit walk-up multi-family community on 7.18 acres (Planning Commission 10-0). Applicant Leah Bergman and Dan Jewell committed to 100% affordable at <=60% AMI if awarded 9% LIHTC credits or at least 25% <=60% AMI with private financing plus bus-shelter pull-offs. Jillian Johnson and Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned whether seeking 9% credits would compete with DHA redevelopment, until Johnson confirmed via text with DHA CEO Anthony Scott that DHA had no 9% application planned for January. Council unanimously approved all three motions 7-0 before adjourning at 10:50 PM.

votes.item_title: Approve Consent Agenda (Excluding Referred Items 4, 21, 22 and Pulled Item 9)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded approving Consent Agenda items 1-3, 5-8, 10-18, and 24. After an initial electronic clicker vote failed to register properly, Mayor O'Neal called a hand vote and recorded 7-0 unanimous passage.

votes.notes: ASR transcribed spoken '4 to 3' as 'for 23'; individual votes were not read aloud by name. votes.notes: ASR transcribed spoken '4 to 3' as 'for 23'; individual member votes were not polled aloud by name.

votes.item_title: Item 19 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 5909 & 6301 Leesville Road
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Leonardo Williams seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for 5909 & 6301 Leesville Road, passing 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 20 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and UEA for East Geer Street Residential
votes.notes: Seconder's specific name was not read aloud after the corrected motion was re-read.

votes.item_title: Item 20 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for East Geer Street Residential (PDR 3.360/CN/RR to RSMD)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded rezoning 7.179 acres in the 2100 block of East Geer Street to Residential Suburban Multi-Family with Development Plan (RSMD) for 90 affordable/workforce units, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 20 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for East Geer Street Residential
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Leonardo Williams seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for East Geer Street Residential, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

disagreements.issue: 5909 & 6301 Leesville Road Mass Grading, Erosion Control ('Tomato Soup'), Well Water, and Growth vs. Housing Supply
disagreements.summary: Following a 9-1 Planning Commission recommendation of denial and over two hours of resident opposition, Council split 4-3 on annexing and rezoning 88 acres on Leesville Road for 330 townhomes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 330 townhomes with strengthened erosion, mass-grading, school, and housing proffers rather than leave the land to expensive well-and-septic estates or industrial uses.
side_a_arguments: Modern stormwater controls necessitate some mass grading, and the applicant added a 50% simultaneous mass-grading cap, 50% open space, $45,000 DPS contribution, and 10 affordable units.
With Durham's rents rising at the third-fastest rate nationally, blocking suburban housing pushes higher-income buyers into existing inner-city neighborhoods.
disagreements.side_b_position: Opponents and dissenting Council members argued mass grading, blasting, flocculants, and strained roads/schools impose severe environmental and taxpayer burdens on Leesville residents.
side_b_arguments: County residents forced onto bottled water due to well sediment and 'tomato soup' creek runoff lack automatic protection or city water access.

Mayor Elaine O'Neal stated she could not vote yes until Council completed its housing deep dive to understand cumulative environmental and infrastructure impacts; DeDreana Freeman argued city taxpayers bear annexation infrastructure costs while inspectors rely on complaint-driven enforcement.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3 by raised hand vote; consistency statement passed 7-0.

disagreements.issue: East Geer Street Residential Competition for Competitive 9% LIHTC Tax Credits
disagreements.summary: While all seven Council members backed the 90-unit East Geer Street affordable/workforce project, Jillian Johnson and Mark-Anthony Middleton initially expressed concern over whether pursuing competitive 9% tax credits would undermine DHA redevelopment plans.
disagreements.side_a_position: Avoid competing with Durham Housing Authority (DHA) for scarce 9% LIHTC credits unless DHA confirms it has no January 2023 application.
side_a_arguments: Long-standing city-DHA coordination seeks to protect 9% tax credits for public housing redevelopment such as Fayette Place.
disagreements.side_b_position: Zoning should not be conditioned on tax-credit choices, and the applicant committed 25% affordable units even if privately financed.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman viewed linking zoning approval to future 9% credit applications as off-putting, and Leah Bergman noted she checked with Community Development and was happy to build privately if DHA needed the credit.
disagreements.resolution: Jillian Johnson confirmed via text message with DHA CEO Anthony Scott that DHA had no 9% application ready for January 2023, and Council approved all three motions 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session August 18, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton absent (excused) and six members present, Council opened on August 18, 2022 with Leonardo Williams and Mayor Elaine O'Neal urging patience and due diligence on a newly submitted Downtown Social District proposal, then approved priority items for the City Manager and City Attorney (6-0 each) and heard Citizen Matters on non-profit wage floors and East End Park engagement. Council debated and gave informal thumbs-up to several Bull City Tenants United recommendations under Item 7 while splitting 2-2 on landlord appliance-repair mandates (referred for staff research), and endorsed Item 8's $147,000 Prescriptions for Repair pilot ($75K Duke, $72K City) alongside Item 9 honoring Dr. Doc J. Jordan and Carrie Thomas Jordan Highway. Council also heard DPD's Q2 Crime Report showing a 5% overall drop in Part I crime alongside youth gun-violence concerns, selected Cooper T. Norris for the Environmental Affairs Board after a tie-break straw poll, directed non-quasi-judicial boards to retain remote meeting flexibility under pre-pandemic attendance rules, and settled the September 6 agenda (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Social District Patience Remarks, Manager & Attorney Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the meeting to order with six members present (Middleton excused) and joined Leonardo Williams in cautioning that DDI's Downtown Social District proposal had just arrived the day prior and required proper due diligence before scheduling. Council approved the City Manager's priority items (increasing VHB/NCPC contract Item 15, scheduling Q2 crime presentation, adding WIOA grant Item 24) 6-0 and accepted City Attorney Kim Rehberg's priority item (scheduling an end-of-meeting remote-board discussion following expiration of Governor Cooper's emergency order) 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Non-Profit Livable Wage Standards & East End/Longmeadow Park Outreach
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Walker Bloom urged Council to tie $18/hour minimum wage standards to ARPA and city nonprofit contracts to address frontline caregiver underpayment. Community resident Henry Chavis thanked Parks and Recreation for East End/Longmeadow Park outreach while urging deeper grassroots engagement with neighborhood elders and churchgoers before finalizing park designs.

agenda_items.title: Bull City Tenants United Housing Code & Eviction Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff presented a package of Bull City Tenants United housing recommendations, earning informal thumbs-up support for uncontested elements such as eviction/code education and enforcement coordination. However, a proposal requiring landlords to repair landlord-provided stoves and refrigerators deadlocked 2-2 in council discussion (with Jillian Johnson and Javiera Caballero in favor, DeDreana Freeman warning landlords might stop supplying appliances altogether, and Leonardo Williams and Mayor O'Neal questioning enforcement capacity and unintended costs), leading Council to direct staff to research legal authority and alternatives separately.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Partial Consensus; Appliance Mandate Referred

agenda_items.title: Prescriptions for Repair Pilot ($147K) & Honorary Fayetteville Street Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff presented Item 8, the Prescriptions for Repair pilot linking Duke Health pediatric clinics, Rebuilding Together of the Triangle, and PEACH to remediate asthma/lead home triggers ($75,000 Duke match plus $72,000 City funding), receiving informal thumbs-up backing with Freeman urging inclusion of minority contractors. For Item 9, council members enthusiastically supported honoring Dr. Doc J. Jordan and Carrie Thomas Jordan on Fayetteville Street after a clarifying historical presentation by descendant/community representatives.

agenda_items.title: DPD 2022 Second Quarter Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Patrice Andrews and analytical manager Jason Sheese presented the Q2 2022 Crime Report showing a 5% overall Part I crime decrease year-to-date despite concerning youth shooting incidents, staffing vacancies, and larceny-from-vehicle spikes. Council members questioned gang coordination, ShotSpotter preparations, and youth intervention strategies.

agenda_items.item_number: Board Nominations, Remote Policy & Settle Agenda
agenda_items.title: Board/Commission Straw Polls, Remote Meeting Guidelines & Settle Sept. 6 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Clerk Diana Schreiber tallied board nominations, with Council conducting a run-off/tie-break selection picking Cooper T. Norris for the Environmental Affairs Board at-large seat after a colleague switched votes. City Attorney Kim Rehberg advised that post-emergency-order rules require quasi-judicial boards and Council to meet in person, and Council reached consensus allowing non-quasi-judicial volunteer boards to keep remote options while reverting to pre-pandemic attendance rules. Council then settled the September 6 agenda 6-0.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items
votes.discussion_detail: With Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton absent (excused), DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded approving the City Manager's priority updates (Item 15 VHB contract amendment amount, Item 18 Q2 crime presentation, Item 23 speaker withdrawal, Item 24 supplemental WIOA grant), passing 6-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Accept City Attorney's Priority Item (Add Remote Boards Policy Discussion)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman seconded accepting City Attorney Kim Rehberg's priority item to hold an end-of-meeting discussion regarding remote meetings for volunteer city boards after Governor Cooper lifted the COVID-19 state of emergency on August 15, passing 6-0 by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 18, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Bull City Tenants United Recommendation Requiring Landlords to Maintain Provided Stoves and Refrigerators
disagreements.summary: While backing other Bull City Tenants United proposals, Council split over adding minimum housing-code mandates requiring landlords to keep supplied appliances in working order.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance the housing-code requirement so landlords who provide appliances cannot leave tenants with broken stoves or refrigerators.
side_a_arguments: Working kitchen appliances are basic habitability needs and tenants already pay rents expecting provided appliances to function.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hold or research alternatives rather than enact a mandate that could prompt landlords to stop supplying appliances or raise compliance burdens.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman warned landlords might simply remove appliances from rental units and force tenants to purchase their own.
Leonardo Williams and Mayor Elaine O'Neal questioned NIS code-enforcement capacity and unintended financial consequences for small landlords and tenants.
disagreements.resolution: Separated from the consensus BCTU items (which advanced to the Sept. 6 consent agenda) and referred back to staff for further legal and policy research.

meetings.title: Durham City Council August 15, 2022 at 7 p.m. (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Elaine O'Neal, the August 15, 2022 Durham City Council regular meeting opened with roll call, unanimous 6-0 approval of excused absences for Council Member Jillian Johnson (absent due to illness) and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton (upcoming absence), and recognition of Neighborhood Improvement Services and NCCU community business-pitch graduates. Mayor O'Neal read Consent Agenda Items 1 through 17 along with Item 27 (Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's first resolution supporting safe and protective measures in Durham schools), though the middle consent vote segment was truncated in the digest. The meeting concluded with a protracted debate on Item 23, the Griffin Residential Tract consolidated annexation and rezoning, centering on stormwater runoff, lack of UDO mass-grading limits, Habitat for Humanity affordable townhouse readiness, and whether pausing approvals constitutes an implicit moratorium. disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 15, 2022 at 7 p.m. (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Griffin Residential Tract Annexation, Mass Grading Limits, Affordable Townhome Readiness, and Development Pause
disagreements.summary: Council deadlocked 3-3 over whether to annex the Griffin Residential Tract and extend utilities amid concerns over stormwater runoff from unlimited mass grading, affordable townhouse execution by Habitat for Humanity, and whether withholding approvals until future Comprehensive Plan policies are adopted constitutes an improper moratorium.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and utility extension rather than imposing an implicit moratorium
side_a_arguments: Council members are elected to make clear yes-or-no decisions on individual proposals rather than halting approvals until future policies are written.
Withholding approvals until unanswered policy questions are resolved amounts to an implicit moratorium.
Design commitments require any affordable townhomes to meet the same material and design standards as market-rate units, and members should debate without alleging opposing votes cause harm.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny annexation pending mass-grading limits, stormwater protections, and deeper housing policy review
side_b_arguments: Current UDO rules place zero limits on mass grading, creating stormwater runoff risks in the Southeast Durham and Falls/Jordan watershed area.
Questions remain about Habitat for Humanity's executive transition, funding, and ability to build affordable townhomes matching market-rate design commitments.
Pausing approval causes no harm and gives Council and the community time to establish updated housing and environmental standards.
disagreements.resolution: Motion 1 failed on a 3-3 tie vote at 02:49:44, leaving the property outside city jurisdiction and rendering the rezoning and consistency statement motions moot.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Work Session May 26, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: On May 26, 2022, the Durham City Council held Day 2 of its FY 2022-23 budget work sessions with all seven seated members present, opening with a moment of silence for children lost to violence across the country. Budget and Management Services Director John Allore introduced presentations covering the public safety portfolio and operational departments, including a Durham Police Department (DPD) overview by Chief Andrews detailing 677 FTEs, Sexual Assault Kit Initiative (SAKI) grant transitions, violent crime trends, and a $6.4 million sworn pay increase. Later in the session, transportation staff presented on regional transit governance and the Durham County Transit Plan, noting a projected fund balance exceeding $100 million alongside staffing and construction-inflation hurdles for project delivery. No formal votes were taken, and Council agreed to reconvene on its June 9 reserve day to hear the remaining four departments.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, and Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the May 26, 2022 budget work session to order at 9:00 a.m. and led a moment of silence for children lost across the country and those in similar situations. The Clerk called the roll, confirming all seven Council members were present, before Budget Director John Allore introduced the Day 2 agenda.

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department FY 2023 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Andrews presented DPD's FY 2023 proposed budget, reporting 677 total sworn and non-sworn FTEs, including 15 frozen officer positions across Districts 4 and 5, Community Services, Organized Crime, and Training, plus four SAKI grant positions. She noted three 2019 SAKI grant positions expire in September 2022—with the cold case victim advocate shifting into an existing non-sworn slot—and reported a $6.4 million funding increase (6.7% operational rise) driven by mid-year sworn pay raises. DPD also reviewed FY 2017–FY 2022 violent crime rates (544 per 100,000 through Q3, projected 725 vs. a 700 target), a 1.7% uptick in robberies, and renewed clearance-rate research with Dr. Cook at Duke University.

agenda_items.title: Regional Transit Funding and Durham County Transit Plan Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation staff reviewed regional transit coordination across Durham, Chapel Hill, Carrboro, Hillsborough, Orange and Chatham counties, the MPO, and GoTriangle, noting that 70% of the 2017 transit plan originally dedicated to Durham-Orange Light Rail became available after its 2019 discontinuation while 15% supports the ongoing commuter rail feasibility study. With the Durham County Transit Plan fund balance projected to exceed $100 million amid 6–9% construction inflation, staff emphasized that securing funded project-delivery positions in the proposed budget is the primary bottleneck. In response to Council questions, staff noted the City holds limited formal voting power over those funds—two of 25 MPO votes and the Mayor's single vote on GoTriangle.

agenda_items.title: Budget Work Session Wrap-Up and Schedule for Reserve Day (June 9)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director John Allore and City Manager Wanda Page thanked department heads and Council for their questions, committing to provide follow-up information before the next budget session. Council confirmed it would reconvene on its reserve day, Thursday, June 9, 2022, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., to hear the remaining four departments (Solid Waste, Parks and Recreation, General Services, and Public Works) before adjourning at 12:54 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Work Session May 25, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: On May 25, 2022, the Durham City Council convened Day 1 of its FY 2022-23 budget work sessions—its first in-person budget retreat in three years—with several members delayed by traffic at call to order before joining the session. Budget and Management Services Director John Allore outlined the schedule covering revenues, the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), human resources, and departmental budgets, noting a potential postponement of Downtown Durham Inc.'s briefing due to a health issue. Allore presented FY 2022-23 General Fund revenue projections featuring a proposed 0.60-cent property tax rate increase, 6% projected property tax growth, and a 13.3% ($5.9 million) jump in sales tax collections. Council members closed with dialogue on retail attraction, local niche businesses, and restaurant labor shortages, taking no formal votes.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Budget Retreat Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the meeting to order after waiting for a quorum due to traffic delays affecting Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council Member Javiera Caballero, and Council Member Leonardo Williams. Budget Director John Allore welcomed Council back to in-person budget sessions for the first time in three years and noted that Downtown Durham Inc.'s presentation might be postponed to the next day due to a health issue.

agenda_items.title: FY 2022-23 Proposed General Fund Revenues Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director John Allore reviewed major General Fund revenue sources—led by property taxes (~50% of General Fund revenue) and sales taxes—building on the prior week's third-quarter financial report. He highlighted a proposed 0.60-cent property tax rate increase, approximately 6% projected property tax growth (above the typical 3–4% baseline), the separate Downtown Business Improvement District (BID) tax, and strong sales tax collections up 13.3% ($5.9 million) over the prior year.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development, Local Business Trends, and Council Closing Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members discussed strategies for retail attraction and small business trends, with Council Member Javiera Caballero noting growing consumer preference for niche local businesses over large chains and Council Member Leonardo Williams citing severe labor shortages in hospitality despite low overall unemployment. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Williams, and other members praised City Manager Wanda Page and Budget Director John Allore for the organized presentations before Mayor O'Neal adjourned the session at 12:37 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session May 19, 2022 at 1 p.m. (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 19, 2022 Durham City Council Work Session, all seven members—including newly appointed Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman at her first work session—heard announcements covering Malcolm X's birthday, Small Business Month, the 51st Bimbé Cultural Arts Festival, and a planned resolution supporting abortion and reproductive rights. Council unanimously approved (7-0) City Manager Wanda Page's priority items for presentations on the FY 2022-23 third-quarter financial report and the 2022 first-quarter crime report, during which Durham Police Department staff reported a 10% increase in Priority 1 calls and slower 6.07-minute response times alongside recruitment adjustments. During board and commission nominations, an initial 3-3 split over appointing Craig Spitzer versus re-advertising was resolved when one member switched to support Spitzer. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton also flagged Procedures Committee review of Monday public hearing comment rules before Council unanimously voted 7-0 to settle the regular meeting agenda.

Staff outlined changes to physical fitness test timing and recruitment from external Basic Law Enforcement Training (BLET) academies that boosted applicant turnout. meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting: ARPA Funding May 18, 2022 at 2 p.m. (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At a special May 18, 2022 meeting dedicated to American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) allocations, Mayor Elaine O'Neal turned facilitation over to Council Members Javiera Caballero and Leonardo Williams, while Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton arrived after roll call in time to join the funding deliberation. Following public comments advocating for affordable housing, green space, the Durham Social Determinants of Health Network, reentry services, and the Harriet Tubman project, Council debated four Excel funding scenarios (Options A–D) prepared by Council Member Jillian Johnson within Council's 50% initial spending cap. While one member initially leaned toward Option B and Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman was open to B or C, Council Member DeDreana Freeman, Council Member Leonardo Williams, and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton favored Option C, resulting in an informal consensus (no formal vote taken) to fund all staff-recommended 'fund' and 'invite to reapply' projects at 70% of their request up to $1 million per project. Williams closed by noting ongoing talks with County Chairwoman Howerton regarding joint investment of the remaining 50% of ARPA funds.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and ARPA Process Recap
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the special meeting to order, with six members present and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton delayed, and handed facilitation to Council Members Javiera Caballero and Leonardo Williams. Caballero recapped the summer 2021 community-driven ARPA process, Council's December 2021 pause after new members took office, Council's decision to allocate up to 50% of ARPA funds in this phase, and Council Member Jillian Johnson's Excel spreadsheet presenting funding Options A–D.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment on ARPA Community Project Proposals
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community speakers advocated for proposed ARPA investments, highlighting affordable housing and green space protection alongside the Durham Social Determinants of Health Network. Additional speakers championed collaborative prisoner reentry programs as a regional and national model and urged support for the Harriet Tubman project serving underrepresented Durham communities.

agenda_items.title: Council Deliberation and Informal Consensus on ARPA Option C
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman highlighted tensions between projects above and below the 24-project staff cutoff, while staff clarified that awards are subject to U.S. Treasury compliance and scope-of-service contract negotiations. After weighing Options B and C within the 50% spending cap, Council reached informal consensus—without taking a formal motion—around Option C to fund all projects staff recommended to 'fund' or 'invite to reapply' at 70% of each request up to a $1 million cap. Council Member Leonardo Williams noted plans to coordinate with Durham County Chairwoman Howerton on a joint second phase for the remaining 50% of funds before adjourning at 3:19 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 16, 2022 at 7 p.m. (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over the May 16, 2022 Durham City Council regular meeting in the absence of Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Council Member DeDreana Freeman, opening with remarks and a moment of silence in solidarity with Buffalo, New York following a racially motivated mass shooting. Due to technical issues with electronic voting tablets, the Clerk conducted all votes by roll call, with the five attending members unanimously granting excused absences (5-0) to O'Neal and Freeman. Council presented a Memorial Day Proclamation to Jonathan Crooms, unanimously passed (5-0) three Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) map-amendment and consistency-statement motions establishing city jurisdiction in the Falls/Jordan Watershed Overlay District B, and held a public hearing before unanimously adopting (5-0) the FY 2023 stormwater fee schedule increases effective July 1, 2022.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Buffalo Solidarity Moment of Silence, and Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton called the meeting to order, condemning the racially motivated shooting in Buffalo, New York and leading a moment of silence in solidarity with Buffalo residents. Following the Pledge of Allegiance, roll call confirmed Middleton, Javiera Caballero, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, Jillian Johnson, and Leonardo Williams present, with Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Council Member DeDreana Freeman absent.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences for Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Council Member DeDreana Freeman
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton noted electronic voting system technical issues requiring roll-call votes and requested excused absences for Mayor O'Neal (traveling) and Council Member Freeman (traveling on city business). Both excused absences were approved unanimously on 5-0 roll-call votes.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item: Memorial Day Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Leonardo Williams read a Memorial Day Proclamation presented to Jonathan Crooms honoring fallen U.S. military personnel. Crooms highlighted Durham County's 375 documented war dead from World War I to the Gulf War era and invited the community to the May 30 annual roll-call ceremony featuring former Durham VA director Paul Crews.

agenda_items.title: Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) Zoning Map Amendment and Consistency Statement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved three related zoning motions by 5-0 roll-call votes, including adopting a UDO amendment shifting property from county RS-M(D) Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Overlay and RS-20 zoning into city RS-M(D) Falls/Jordan Watershed Overlay District B (F/J-B) jurisdiction and adopting the NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement. Afterward, Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman asked staff where residents can look up zoning acronyms, and staff pointed to full definitions in staff reports, ordinances, and the Development Services Center.

agenda_items.title: General Business Item 22: FY 2023 Stormwater Rates Public Hearing and Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Paul Wiepke presented proposed FY 2023 stormwater rate increases effective July 1, 2022: +$0.45/month for Tier 1 residential ($4.20/mo), +$0.94/month for Tier 2 ($8.70/mo), +$1.87/month for Tier 3 ($17.42/mo), and +$0.94 per 2,400 sq. ft. of impervious surface for other residential/non-residential customers ($8.70/mo). After opening and closing the public hearing with no speakers, Council unanimously adopted the revised fee schedule ordinance 5-0 and adjourned at 8:53 p.m.

votes.item_title: Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment Ordinance (RS-M(D) / RS-20 County to RS-M(D) F/J-B City Jurisdiction)

votes.discussion_detail: Ordinance taking property out of county RS-M(D) Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Overlay and RS-20 districts and establishing RS-M(D) Falls/Jordan Watershed Overlay District B (F/J-B) city jurisdiction.

votes.item_title: Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Zoning Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Motion 3 of 3 on the zoning item.

votes.item_title: General Business Item 22: Adopt Ordinance Revising FY 2023 Stormwater Rates Effective July 1, 2022
votes.notes: Followed public hearing with zero speakers.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted revised stormwater fee schedule increasing Tier 1 residential rates by $0.45/mo, Tier 2 by $0.94/mo, Tier 3 by $1.87/mo, and non-residential/other residential by $0.94 per 2,400 sq. ft. impervious surface.

meetings.search_blob: durham city council may 16, 2022 at 7 p.m. (livestream) mark-anthony middleton mayor pro tempore mark-anthony middleton presided over the may 16, 2022 durham city council regular meeting in the absence of mayor elaine o'neal and council member dedreana freeman, opening with remarks and a moment of silence in solidarity with buffalo, new york following a racially motivated mass shooting. due to technical issues with electronic voting tablets, the clerk conducted all votes by roll call, with the five attending members unanimously granting excused absences (5-0) to o'neal and freeman. council presented a memorial day proclamation to jonathan crooms, unanimously passed (5-0) three unified development ordinance (udo) map-amendment and consistency-statement motions establishing city jurisdiction in the falls/jordan watershed overlay district b, and held a public hearing before unanimously adopting (5-0) the fy 2023 stormwater fee schedule increases effective july 1, 2022. budget & taxes governance & transparency zoning & development (scad) call to order, buffalo solidarity moment of silence, and roll call excused absences for mayor elaine o'neal and council member dedreana freeman ceremonial item: memorial day proclamation unified development ordinance (udo) zoning map amendment and consistency statement general business item 22: fy 2023 stormwater rates public hearing and ordinance grant excused absence to mayor elaine o'neal grant excused absence to council member dedreana freeman zoning/annexation action — motion 1 (preceding udo ordinance) adopt udo zoning map amendment ordinance (rs-m(d) / rs-20 county to rs-m(d) f/j-b city jurisdiction) adopt ncgs 160d-605 zoning consistency statement general business item 22: adopt ordinance revising fy 2023 stormwater rates effective july 1, 2022
